docs.title: Decayed linear recurrence
docs.text:
decay_rnn · ab.build("decay_rnn")

Decayed linear recurrence: H_t = gamma H_{t-1} + psi(k_t) v_t^T.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.DecayRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/decay_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences (rows "Retention", "GLA / Mamba-2"). A_t = gamma Id with a fixed gamma < 1 is retention (RetNet); a data-dependent scalar or diagonal gate gives Mamba-2, GLA, HGRN2, RWKV-5/6 and the mLSTM. The weights on the original positions are

w_{tj} = gamma^{(t - j)} <phi(q_t), psi(k_j)>,    j <= t,

an exponential recency prior multiplying a rank-r content term.

Decay restores boundedness without restoring normalization: the effective mass sum_i prod_{u>i} gamma_u is bounded by 1/(1 - gamma) rather than growing with n, so the output cannot blow up with context length, but it is still not an expectation under a probability measure (set normalize=True to recover one). This is the distinction sec:memory-state draws between "restoring boundedness" and "restoring the contract".

State size is r x d_v regardless of gamma, so sweeping gamma at fixed state separates recency from capacity — which is what study S6 needs.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
parameter default decay 0.9 feature 'elu' normalize False 
ab.describe("decay_rnn")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: decay, gate, mass.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = d
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv + m * n,
            "state_bytes": r * dv * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 17,825,792 268,435,456 0.0664× state_bytes 8,192 262,144 0.0312× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("decay_rnn", decay=0.9, feature='elu')
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with decay_rnn removed.

changes the same object — recurrent delta_rnn, gla, hgrn2, hyena, linear_rnn, lru, mega, mlstm, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, recurrent only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, gqa, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, lowrank_ot, mla, otke, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, sinkhorn, unbalanced_sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, modify only

Open the browser with decay_rnn selected and tick up to three more to see them in columns. Every row there is one the registry declares, and the rows the selected methods agree on fold away.

docs.title: DeltaNet
docs.text:
delta_rnn · ab.build("delta_rnn")

DeltaNet: the delta-rule update on a fast-weight memory.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.DeltaRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/delta_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, eq:memory-delta, tab:memory-recurrences (row "DeltaNet"). The transition is a rank-one correction rather than a decay:

H_t = (I - beta_t psi_t psi_t^T) H_{t-1} + beta_t psi_t v_t^T,    psi_t = psi(k_t),
y_hat_t = H_t^T phi(q_t),

which is exactly one gradient step of size beta_t on the per-token regression loss L_t(H) = 1/2 ||H^T psi_t - v_t||^2 (Widrow–Hoff). Plain linear attention is a gradient step on the linear loss -<H^T psi_t, v_t>, which never saturates and so never corrects interference between non-orthogonal keys; the delta rule does. That is the whole capacity argument: at a fixed state of r x d_v, the delta rule stores more distinguishable associations than the additive recurrence, which is what study S6 measures.

The regression view also identifies the operator. Softmax attention is a Nadaraya–Watson estimator that never leaves the convex hull of the stored values; the delta rule fits a global parametric regression of v on psi(k) online and returns arbitrary linear combinations. It is a new operator and is judged by downstream quality, not by fidelity to y(q).

Weights. H_t is linear in V, so H_t = M_t V for an r x n coefficient matrix obeying the same recurrence driven by the basis vectors, M_t = (I - beta psi_t psi_t^T) M_{t-1} + beta psi_t e_t^T. Running it gives the exact weights w_{tj} = <phi(q_t), M_t[:, j]> at a cost of O(n^2 r), which is the price of exposing pi_hat on the original positions. psi is l2-normalized, as in DeltaNet, so that I - beta psi psi^T is a contraction for beta in (0, 2).

Note on notation: DESIGN.md writes the update as H_{t-1}(I - beta phi phi^T), which is the same map with H transposed (d_v x r). This file follows the paper's eq:memory-delta with H in R^{r x d_v}.

Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):

docs.title: Partial-assignment attention
docs.text:
dustbin_sinkhorn · ab.build("dustbin_sinkhorn")

Partial-assignment attention: Sinkhorn on a score matrix with a dustbin.

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.DustbinSinkhornAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/dustbin_sinkhorn.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot, "Unbalanced relaxation". A doubly stochastic plan forces every query to spend all of its mass on real keys and every key to receive exactly its share. The discrete way to buy slack is the one SuperGlue uses for unmatchable keypoints (Sarlin et al. 2020, eq. 8-9): augment the scores with one extra row and one extra column — a dustbin — filled with a single scalar z,

Sbar[i, j]   = beta <q_i, k_j> / eps      i <= m, j <= n
Sbar[i, n+1] = Sbar[m+1, j] = Sbar[m+1, n+1] = z / eps,

and prescribe marginals that give the bin exactly the surplus capacity,

a = [1_m, n] / (m + n),      b = [1_n, m] / (m + n),

so that both sides carry unit total mass. Sinkhorn on exp(Sbar) then returns a partial assignment: the m x n block is a coupling of what was matched, and the dustbin entries hold what was not.

As an attention operator the conditional is read off the augmented row and renormalized over the real keys. Because the plan is still of Gibbs form, this is exact rather than a projection:

pi_hat_i(j) = softmax_j ( s_ij + g_j ),        j = 1 .. n,

with g the column potential restricted to the real keys — prop:ot-conditional again, with the tilt now computed in the presence of the bin. The mass the query sent to the bin, extras["dustbin_mass"], is the quantity renormalization removes; it is the abstention the operator permits, and it is reported rather than hidden.

Two limits bracket the method. As z -> -infinity the bin becomes unattractive, the surplus is absorbed by the bin-to-bin cell, and the real block approaches the doubly stochastic plan of sinkhorn. As z grows, queries divert mass to the bin and dustbin_mass -> 1; the renormalized conditional stays finite and tends to the conditional induced by the bin row's own tilt. The default dustbin = 0.0 sits between them; in SuperGlue z is a learned parameter, which is the only sense in which this operator has one — it is a scalar, and the operator is meaningful at any value of it, so trainable stays False.

One cost of the deep-bin limit is worth recording, because it is not visible in the construction. As z falls, the bin's entries vanish relative to the real block and the augmented matrix loses total support in the sense of Sinkhorn (1967); the scaling iterations then give up their geometric rate. Measured at z = -40 the distance to the balanced plan decays like 1/n_iter, so recovering sinkhorn this way costs thousands of iterations where sinkhorn itself needs tens. At the useful values of z — those where abstention is actually happening — convergence is geometric and the default n_iter = 20 is ample.

This is the discrete counterpart of unbalanced_sinkhorn: a hard constraint with an escape hatch, rather than a soft penalty. sec:ot lists both, alongside explicit register tokens, as ways to keep abstention under a column constraint.

Not causal: prop:ot-causal. The dustbin does relax the marginals — the compatibility inequality eq:ot-hall is no longer tight — but the slack it provides is a single lump, not the position-decreasing column marginal that the proposition says would be needed, and the plan of a prefix still changes when a token arrives.

docs.title: ESPFormer
docs.text:
espformer · ab.build("espformer")

ESPFormer: doubly stochastic attention from expected sliced transport plans.

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.ESPFormerAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/espformer.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot, "Doubly stochastic attention in transformers". Sinkformers reach the column constraint by iterating eq:ot-sinkhorn; the iteration is sequential, and its Hilbert-metric rate degrades exponentially in ||c||_inf / eps. ESPFormer — Shahbazi et al. (2025), building on the expected sliced transport plan of Liu et al. (2025) — reaches it in a single pass instead, by averaging one-dimensional transport plans.

The construction, for one slice theta in R^d:

  1. project the queries and the keys on theta: q_i^theta = <q_i, theta>, k_j^theta = <k_j, theta>;
  2. between two uniform measures on the line the optimal plan is the monotone rearrangement: sort both sides and match rank to rank. With A and B the (descending) sorting permutations of the projected queries and keys,
   U_theta = (1/m) A^T I B,

where I is the m x n rank-to-rank coupling (eq:ot-nwcorner in spirit: the north-west-corner plan between the uniform marginals 1/m and 1/n, with rows rescaled to sum to one). I is the identity when m == n, which is the form stated in the paper. U_theta has row marginal 1/m and column marginal 1/n: it is a transport plan, not a row normalization; 3. the plans of the individual slices are averaged with weights that favour the cheap slices,

   G = sum_l sigma_l U_{theta_l},
   sigma_l = softmax_l( -tau_slice * sum_ij C_ij [U_{theta_l}]_ij ),
   C_ij = ||beta q_i - beta k_j||^2 .

A convex combination of couplings in Pi(nu, mubar) is again in Pi(nu, mubar), so G is doubly stochastic exactly, with no iteration at all. The attention operator is pi_hat = m G (row-stochastic) and y = pi_hat v.

Soft sorting. argsort has zero gradient almost everywhere, so A and B are replaced by SoftSort_t (Prillo and Eisenschlos, 2020), SoftSort_t(x)[r, i] = softmax_i( -(x_i - sort(x)_r)^2 / t ). This is the one place where the construction stops being exact: at finite t the relaxed A is row-stochastic but not a permutation, so its column sums — and hence the row sums of G — deviate from one. The operator is renormalized here so that pi_hat is a probability measure, and the deviation that was removed is reported as extras["row_sum_error"]. It goes to zero as t -> 0; the test suite checks that it does.

Two conventions, stated so that numbers transfer. The slice cost here is that of the unit-mass plan U_theta, as in the paper; the released code omits the 1/n and so weights the slices with an inverse temperature larger by that factor (its default is 10 against the paper's 0.1). And the paper's Algorithm 1 uses the squared Euclidean cost while the released code uses the distance itself; both are available through cost=, with the paper's as the default. Neither choice changes the support of the operator, only how sharply the cheap slices are preferred. Under those two conventions extras["plan"] reproduces the authors' released module bit for bit; tests/test_coupling_transport.py writes out that computation and checks it.

No key potential. prop:ot-conditional says the entropic-OT conditional is softmax tilted by one number per key. ESP's plan is a mixture of permutations, not a Gibbs kernel exp(s + f + g), so no such psi exists and extras deliberately contains no "potential": study S7's tilt analysis does not apply to it. What it does expose — gamma, row_marginal, col_marginal, marginal_error — matches sinkhorn, so the marginal diagnostics are shared.

Cost. Not sub-quadratic, and not claimed to be. The paper reports O(N_sl * n(n + d)) for N_sl slices and credits the method with being parallel over slices where Sinkhorn is sequential over iterations. In this reference implementation the dominant term is larger still: A^T I B is a product of dense m x m, m x n and n x n matrices once the sort is relaxed, so forming the N_sl plans costs O(N_sl * mn(m + n)). A hard sort would make the product a permutation composition and recover the quoted figure, at the price of the gradient the soft sort exists to provide. cost() reports what this file executes.

Slices. The paper sets Theta = I_{d x d} — axis-aligned slices, so that the mechanism adds no parameters at all; that is the default here (n_slices=None) and the reason trainable = False. Its Table 6 ablates learnable slicers, which help when the number of slices is small; n_slices=L draws L directions uniformly on the sphere through a seeded generator, which is that ablation's initialization but not its training.

Not causal, for the reason every doubly stochastic operator is not: prop:ot-causal, a lower-triangular matrix with equal row and column sums is diagonal. Sorting is in any case a global operation over the sequence.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_slices None tau 0.001 tau_slice 0.1 cost 'sqeuclidean' seed 0

n_slices: None for the paper's axis-aligned Theta = I (d slices), or an integer for that many random directions on the sphere. tau: SoftSort temperature (the paper's t = 1e-3); -> 0 is a hard sort. tau_slice: inverse temperature of the slice weights (the paper's tau = 0.1), applied to the cost of the unit-mass plan U_theta. 0 averages the slices. cost: 'sqeuclidean' (Algorithm 1) or 'euclidean' (the released code).

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A fixed-point iteration over the whole matrix is not a kernel call, and the normalisation it computes is not per-query.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: col_marginal, gamma, marginal_error, n_slices, plan, row_marginal, row_sum_error, slice_cost, slice_weights, slices, target_col, target_row.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """What this file executes, not the quoted asymptotics.

    ``n_sl`` soft sorts (``m^2 + n^2`` each), ``n_sl`` triple products
    ``A^T (I B)`` (``mn(m + n)`` each), the cost matrix, and one ``m x n`` apply.
    The ``mn(m + n)`` term is the price of relaxing the sort: with hard
    permutations the same product is a relabelling in ``O(mn)`` and the total
    collapses to the paper's ``O(n_sl * n(n + d))``.
    """
    n_sl = self.n_slices if self.n_slices is not None else d
    return {"flops": 2 * n_sl * (m + n) * d + n_sl * (m * m + n * n)
                     + 2 * n_sl * m * n * (m + n) + 3 * m * n + 2 * m * n * dv,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv
                            + n_sl * m * n) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 275,166,265,344 268,435,456 1.03e+03× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 134,742,016 4,718,592 28.6×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("espformer", tau=0.001, tau_slice=0.1)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

ESPFormerAttention(name='espformer', category='coupling', objective='modify', backend='reference', cost='sqeuclidean', n_slices=None, seed=0, tau=0.001, tau_slice=0.1)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[col_marginal, gamma, marginal_error, n_slices, plan, row_marginal, row_sum_error, slice_cost, slice_weights, slices, target_col, target_row], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
extras: ['col_marginal', 'gamma', 'marginal_error', 'n_slices', 'plan', 'row_marginal', 'row_sum_error', 'slice_cost', 'slice_weights', 'slices', 'target_col', 'target_row']

docs.title: Ada-KV
docs.text:
evict_adakv · ab.build("evict_adakv")

Ada-KV: one eviction budget for the whole layer, allocated across heads.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.AdaKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_adakv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, prop:compress-noeviction. SnapKV, H2O and PyramidKV give every head of a layer the same cache size. Ada-KV observes that heads differ enormously in how concentrated their attention is — a head whose mass sits on three tokens wastes a budget of sixty, while a diffuse head is crippled by it — and that the top-k eviction rule is itself the minimiser of an upper bound on the output perturbation. Allocating the layer's total budget H b so as to minimise that bound jointly over heads turns out to be a single global selection:

take the `H b` largest observation scores over the concatenation of all heads,
let `f_h` be how many of them belong to head `h`, and give head `h` a cache
of size `f_h`.

The released code then blends that with the uniform allocation through a safeguard alpha, b_h = round((1 - alpha) f_h + alpha b), which stops a head from being starved to the point where the bound's assumptions stop holding. alpha = 1 is uniform allocation and recovers SnapKV head for head; alpha = 0 is the raw argmin. Either way sum_h b_h = H b up to rounding: the budget is moved between heads, never increased, and tests/test_compress_evict.py checks it.

Heads are coupled, and that is the mechanism. The method declares head_independent = False: perturbing head 1's keys moves head 2's cache size, because they are drawing on one pool. This is the same kind of honest declaration gqa and mla make, for a different reason — they share the stored K/V, Ada-KV shares the budget.

Semantics: eviction, not restriction. As in SnapKV the support is fixed once from the observation window and then serves every query, so a query outside that window is answered from a cache that was pruned without knowing what it would ask. Hence supports_causal = False, and hence prop:compress-noeviction: adaptive allocation buys a better average, not a uniform guarantee.

Exact limit: budget = None (nothing is evicted).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent no it shares \(K\)/\(V\) across query heads, so heads are not independent. trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default budget 8 floor_alpha 0.2 obs 4 pool 3 pooling 'max' recent 2

budget is the per-head average; floor_alpha = 1 recovers SnapKV.

ab.describe("evict_adakv")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("evict_adakv").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: adaptive_budget, budget, chi2, eps, head_budget, k_realized, obs, pooled_scores, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = max(1, min(self.budget or n, n))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + self.obs * n * d,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,359,296 268,435,456 0.00879× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 2,359,296 4,718,592 0.5×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("evict_adakv", budget=8, floor_alpha=0.2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["evict_adakv"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"evict_adakv": {'budget': 8, 'floor_alpha': 0.2}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: H2O
docs.text:
evict_h2o · ab.build("evict_h2o")

H2O: accumulated-attention heavy-hitter eviction plus a recent window.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.H2OAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_h2o.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, prop:compress-noeviction. Eviction is a restriction whose set is chosen before the queries that will use it exist, and the sets are nested: S_{t+1} subset S_t union {t+1}. A deleted token is gone for every future query, so prop:compress-noeviction says no query-oblivious rule has a uniform guarantee — for any retained S and any evicted j, the query q = tau k_j drives eps_q -> 1 while y_hat stays in conv{v_i : i in S}.

H2O estimates the future-query distribution nu by the empirical distribution of past queries: token j is scored by sum_{t' <= t} pi_{q_{t'}}(j), and the lowest-scoring non-recent token is dropped whenever the cache exceeds its budget. This file runs that process literally, one query at a time, which is why it is causal: the state at step t depends on keys and queries up to t only.

In non-causal mode the whole context is admitted at the first step and the same accumulate-and-evict loop runs over the queries in order; the semantics are then "a streaming cache served by a fixed context".

Exact limit: budget = None (no eviction).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default budget 8 recent 2

budget: cache size; recent: most recent positions never evicted.

ab.describe("evict_h2o")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("evict_h2o").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: accumulated, budget, chi2, eps, k_realized, recent, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = min(self.budget or n, n)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + m * b,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + b * 4,   # +accumulated scores
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,105,344 268,435,456 0.00784× state_bytes 2,080 262,144 0.00793× bytes_moved 2,359,296 4,718,592 0.5×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("evict_h2o", budget=8, recent=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["evict_h2o"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"evict_h2o": {'budget': 8, 'recent': 2}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: PyramidKV
docs.text:
evict_pyramidkv · ab.build("evict_pyramidkv")

PyramidKV: the eviction budget is allocated across layers, not uniformly.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.PyramidKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_pyramidkv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, prop:compress-noeviction. SnapKV and H2O give every layer the same cache size. PyramidKV observes that attention concentrates as depth grows — lower layers spread mass broadly, upper layers funnel it onto a few tokens — and so spends the same total budget unevenly: the per-layer budgets form a decreasing arithmetic sequence, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top.

base   = budget - recent                      # what a uniform scheme would give
lo     = base // beta,   hi = 2 base - lo     # the ends of the sequence
b^(l)  = hi - l (hi - lo) / (L - 1) + recent

The mean of the sequence is base, so the allocation moves cache between layers rather than buying more of it; pyramid_budgets returns the whole schedule and tests/test_compress_evict.py checks the conservation. The official implementation uses integer floor division for the step, which loses up to one token per layer; the exact arithmetic sequence is used here so that the conservation is a statement and not an approximation.

A single attention call has no notion of depth, so the layer is a config key: ab.build("evict_pyramidkv", layer=l, n_layers=L) is layer l of the stack, and a sweep over l is what exhibits the pyramid. Within a layer the selection is SnapKV's — the last obs queries score the prompt tokens, a 1-D pooling of width pool keeps neighbourhoods rather than isolated tokens, and the recent window is always resident. pooling='max' is the default here, which is what PyramidKV and SnapKV's released code use; evict_snapkv in this package uses average pooling, so the pair isolates the effect of the pooling operator.

Semantics: eviction, not restriction. The support is chosen once, from the observation window, and the same support then serves every query — including the queries that are not in that window and whose own top-b is a different set. The context those queries would have needed is gone, which is why the method declares supports_causal = False: query 0's support depends on query m-1, and no causal mask can express that. tests/test_compress_evict.py measures the gap against the per-query restriction topk at the same budget; it is the price of deleting rather than hiding, and prop:compress-noeviction says no budget makes it uniformly small.

Exact limit: budget = None (every layer keeps everything).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default budget 8 n_layers 4 layer 0 beta 4 obs 4 pool 3 pooling 'max' recent 2

budget is the uniform budget the pyramid redistributes; layer of n_layers picks this call's share of it.

ab.describe("evict_pyramidkv")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("evict_pyramidkv").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: budget, chi2, eps, k_realized, layer_budgets, obs, pooled_scores, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = self._layer_budgets(n)[self.layer]
    b = max(1, min(b if b is not None else n, n))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + self.obs * n * d,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 3,670,016 268,435,456 0.0137× state_bytes 3,328 262,144 0.0127× bytes_moved 3,670,016 4,718,592 0.778×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("evict_pyramidkv", budget=8, n_layers=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["evict_pyramidkv"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"evict_pyramidkv": {'budget': 8, 'n_layers': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

PyramidKVAttention(name='evict_pyramidkv', category='compress', objective='approximate', backend='reference', beta=4, budget=8, layer=0, n_layers=4, obs=4, pool=3, pooling='max', recent=2)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[budget, chi2, eps, k_realized, layer_budgets, obs, pooled_scores, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)

docs.title: SnapKV
docs.text:
evict_snapkv · ab.build("evict_snapkv")

SnapKV: prompt-token scores pooled over an observation window.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.SnapKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_snapkv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict ("Estimating importance from past queries"). SnapKV scores prompt tokens with the attention of the last obs prompt queries, applies a 1-D pooling of width pool along the key axis so that whole local neighbourhoods are kept rather than isolated tokens, keeps the top budget - recent of them, and adds the recent window. The compressed cache then serves all subsequent decoding queries.

This works when the question ends the prompt — the observation window is then a good sample of nu in eq:compress-evict-objective — and degrades when it arrives earlier.

Not causal, deliberately. The support is chosen after seeing the whole prompt and is then applied to every query, including earlier ones. That is what SnapKV does in a prefill-then-decode pipeline, and it cannot be expressed as a causally masked single forward pass: query 0's support would depend on query m-1. Declaring supports_causal = False records the fact rather than hiding it behind a mask.

Exact limit: budget = None.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default budget 8 obs 4 pool 3 recent 2 
ab.describe("evict_snapkv")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("evict_snapkv").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: budget, chi2, eps, k_realized, obs, pooled_scores, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = min(self.budget or n, n)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + self.obs * n * d,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,359,296 268,435,456 0.00879× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 2,359,296 4,718,592 0.5×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("evict_snapkv", budget=8, obs=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["evict_snapkv"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"evict_snapkv": {'budget': 8, 'obs': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: TOVA
docs.text:
evict_tova · ab.build("evict_tova")

TOVA: drop the token the current query cares least about, one per step.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.TOVAAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_tova.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, prop:compress-noeviction. Reading a decoder as a multi-state RNN, the KV cache is the state and a cache policy is a rule for keeping it bounded. TOVA is the simplest non-trivial such rule: at every step the new token is admitted, and if the cache is over budget the state with the smallest weight under the query that just arrived is deleted. No accumulation over history (that is evict_h2o), no protected recent window (that is sink_window), no observation window (that is evict_snapkv): one query decides, once, and the decision is permanent.

S_0 = {0},   S_t = topkeep_{b}( S_{t-1} u {t}; pi_{q_t} ),   S_t \ {t} subset S_{t-1}

Semantics: eviction, and the file is built so that this is visible. The supports are produced by a loop over queries in order, so the set serving query t was fixed by queries <= t and nothing later can restore what they threw away. Two consequences are tested in tests/test_compress_evict.py rather than asserted here:

  • the supports are nested — S_{t+1} subset S_t u {t+1}. window and sink_window are nested too, which is exactly why they are listed in both restrict/ and sec:compress-evict; the content-dependent selectors are not, because a restriction recomputes its set per query and is free to come back to a position it ignored a step ago. topk at the same budget is the comparison;
  • at equal budget the error against dense softmax is larger than topk's, and the gap grows along the query axis: early queries are served by a cache that still holds almost everything, late ones by a cache pruned long before their question was asked. That gap is the whole content of prop:compress-noeviction — restriction hides context, eviction destroys it.

The current position is the one protection the policy keeps, so that no row is ever left with an empty support (DESIGN.md Sec. 4, rule 10); TOVA keeps it in practice anyway, since a token's own key usually dominates its row. extras['evicted_at'] records the step at which each position was deleted, or -1 if it survived, which is the permanence made inspectable.

In non-causal mode the whole context is admitted at the first step and the same evict-per-query loop runs over the queries in order: "a streaming cache served by a fixed context", the convention evict_h2o also uses.

Exact limit: budget = None (nothing is ever evicted).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("evict_tova").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: budget, chi2, eps, evicted_at, k_realized, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = max(1, min(self.budget or n, n))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + m * b,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,105,344 268,435,456 0.00784× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 2,359,296 4,718,592 0.5×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("evict_tova", budget=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["evict_tova"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"evict_tova": {'budget': 8}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: FAVOR++
docs.text:
favorpp · ab.build("favorpp")

FAVOR++: optimal positive random features for the softmax kernel.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.FAVORPlusPlusAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/favorpp.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-rf. FAVOR+ (performer) is one point of a much larger family. With qt = q / d^{1/4}, kt = k / d^{1/4} and g(q,x) = exp(<qt, kt_x>), Likhosherstov et al. (2022) consider the generalized exponential random features

f_A(omega, u) = D exp(A ||omega||^2 + B omega^T u + C ||u||^2),   omega ~ N(0, I_d),

and show (their Thm. 3.1) that E[f_A(omega,qt) f_A(omega,kt)] = g exactly when

B = sqrt(1 - 4A),   C = -1/2,   D = (1 - 4A)^{d/4},   A < 1/4.

A = 0 gives B = D = 1 and recovers FAVOR+ verbatim, so this file contains performer as the special case a = 0. Every other A is an equally unbiased estimator with a different variance, and Thm. 3.3 minimises that variance in closed form: for a pair (qt, kt) with S = ||qt + kt||^2 the optimum is

A* = (1 - 1/rho*) / 8,
rho* = (sqrt((2S + d)^2 + 8 d S) - 2S - d) / (4 S),

equivalently, writing lam = S / d for the mean eigenvalue of the pair covariance,

A* = (1 - 2 lam - sqrt((2 lam + 1)^2 + 8 lam)) / 16

— the two expressions are identical after rationalising 1/rho*. The second is the form optimal_a uses and the form favorsharp generalises one eigendirection at a time. A* <= 0 always, and A* -> 0 as S -> 0: FAVOR+ is optimal only in the small-logit limit, and the gain grows without bound with the logit scale — the regime in which FAVOR+'s relative variance exp(S) - 1 explodes.

Where A comes from here. A* depends on the pair. The paper fixes one A per layer from batch averages of ||x + y||^2 (their Eq. 8), which is not a causal function of the context and would make the operator leak — the normalizer of an early query would move when a later key changed. This file instead conditions the statistic on each query's visible support,

S_i = ||qt_i||^2 + mean_{j visible to i} ||kt_j||^2 + 2 <qt_i, mean_{j} kt_j>,

which is the same average restricted to the pairs that query actually estimates: the paper averages over i as well, so the two agree exactly at m = 1 (decoding) and otherwise differ only by that conditioning. It is exactly causal and exactly head-independent. Unbiasedness is untouched: A is a deterministic function of the data and independent of omega, so E_omega[g_hat] = g for whatever A is chosen. Pass a=<float> to pin A instead and recover the separable, layer-constant form (a = 0 is performer, bit for bit).

cost reports that deployed separable form, as performer does; the query-conditioned statistic used here costs an extra O(m n r) and is a property of this reference implementation, not of the method.

Like FAVOR+ the estimator is positive, so pi_hat is a genuine probability measure, and like FAVOR+ it is a ratio of two unbiased estimators and therefore biased at O(1/r): there is no finite r at which it is exact, hence convergence_configs rather than a limit_config.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
parameter default r 64 a None orthogonal True seed 0

a = None fits A* from the visible support; a float pins A.

ab.describe("favorpp")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

>>> ab.get_class("favorpp").convergence_configs()
[{'r': 8}, {'r': 32}, {'r': 128}, {'r': 512}]

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: A, B, Z_rel, log_g_hat, r.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.r
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv
                     + 2 * (m + n) * d,            # the O(Ld) statistic, Eq. 8
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 33,816,576 268,435,456 0.126× state_bytes 8,320 262,144 0.0317× bytes_moved 532,608 4,718,592 0.113×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("favorpp", r=64, orthogonal=True)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["favorpp"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"favorpp": {'r': 64, 'orthogonal': True}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

FAVORPlusPlusAttention(name='favorpp', category='interaction', objective='approximate', backend='reference', a=None, orthogonal=True, r=64, seed=0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[A, B, Z_rel, log_g_hat, r], dtype=float32, device=cpu)

docs.title: FAVOR
docs.text:
favorsharp · ab.build("favorsharp")

FAVOR#: dense-exponential random features, the anisotropic optimum.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.FAVORSharpAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/favorsharp.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-rf. favorpp optimises one scalar A over the family D exp(A ||omega||^2 + B omega^T u + C ||u||^2). Likhosherstov et al. (2023) let the quadratic form be a full matrix — dense-exponential random features —

f(omega, u) = D exp(omega^T A omega + omega^T B u + u^T C u),   omega ~ N(0, I_d),

and their Thm. 4.1 gives unbiasedness for g(q,x) = exp(<qt, kt_x>) iff

8A < I,   B^T (I - 4A)^{-1} B = I,   C = -1/2 B^T (I - 4A)^{-1} B,
D = det(I - 4A)^{1/4},

which for the symmetric choice B^(1) = B^(2) = B collapses to C = -I/2. The optimum of the shifted log-variance over the pair set (their Thm. 4.3) is the eigendecomposition of the pair covariance

Sigma = mean_{i,j} (qt_i + kt_j)(qt_i + kt_j)^T
      = M^(1) + mu^(4) (mu^(5))^T + mu^(5) (mu^(4))^T + M^(2) = Q Lam Q^T,

after which, with attnbank.methods.interaction.favorpp.optimal_a applied to each eigenvalue,

A = diag(A*(Lam_1), ..., A*(Lam_d)),   B = (I - 4A)^{1/2} Q^T,
C = -I/2,   D = det(I - 4A)^{1/4} = prod_l (1 - 4 A_ll)^{1/4}.

So FAVOR# is FAVOR++ run independently in each eigendirection of Sigma, and FAVOR++ is FAVOR# with every eigenvalue replaced by their mean tr(Sigma)/d: the two closed forms are the same scalar map A*, which is why optimal_a lives in one place and is used by both. At Sigma = 0 it collapses further still: A = 0, B = Q^T is an orthogonal rotation, and Q omega is again N(0, I_d), so the estimator is FAVOR+ in distribution.

Because Sigma is a mean of outer products it is positive semidefinite, so every Lam_l >= 0, every A*(Lam_l) <= 0 and 1 - 4A > 0: the feature map is real and strictly positive, and pi_hat is a probability measure.

Causality. As in favorpp, the statistic is conditioned on each query's visible support — Sigma_i = qt_i qt_i^T + qt_i ybar_i^T + ybar_i qt_i^T + M2_i with ybar_i, M2_i the prefix means of kt_j and kt_j kt_j^T — so the operator is exactly causal and head-independent, and unbiasedness is untouched because Sigma does not depend on omega. The statistic and the eigendecomposition are done in float64 so that the choice of basis, which a sign flip of an eigenvector would otherwise make dtype-dependent, is identical in every precision; eigenvector signs are additionally canonicalised (largest-magnitude entry positive), which the estimator's distribution is invariant to.

The per-query O(d^3) eigendecomposition is the price of exact causality and is a property of this reference implementation; cost reports the deployed form, in which Sigma is a layer constant fitted once (O(L d^2 + d^3)) and the features are separable.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

>>> ab.get_class("favorsharp").convergence_configs()
[{'r': 8}, {'r': 32}, {'r': 128}, {'r': 512}]

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: A_diag, Z_rel, eigenvalues, log_g_hat, r.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.r
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv
                     + (m + n) * d * d + d ** 3,     # the pair covariance and its eigh
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 42,205,184 268,435,456 0.157× state_bytes 8,320 262,144 0.0317× bytes_moved 532,608 4,718,592 0.113×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("favorsharp", r=64, orthogonal=True)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["favorsharp"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"favorsharp": {'r': 64, 'orthogonal': True}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

FAVORSharpAttention(name='favorsharp', category='interaction', objective='approximate', backend='reference', orthogonal=True, r=64, seed=0)

docs.title: FlashAttention
docs.text:
flash · ab.build("flash")

FlashAttention: tiled online softmax (sec:exact, sec:exact-tiling).

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective accelerate — same operator, exact up to floating point; only the evaluation changes class attnbank.FlashAttention, attnbank/methods/exact/flash.py monograph sec:exact

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues acceleration: the operator is the reference operator, exact up to floating point. The only question worth asking of it is where exactness stops.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
The operator is unchanged. For a block J of key indices the partial state is

sigma_J = (a_J, l_J, u_J),
a_J = max_{j in J} s_j,  l_J = sum_{j in J} e^{s_j - a_J},  u_J = sum_{j in J} e^{s_j - a_J} v_j,

with merge (eq:exact-merge)

(a1,l1,u1) + (a2,l2,u2) = (a, e^{a1-a} l1 + e^{a2-a} l2, e^{a1-a} u1 + e^{a2-a} u2),
a = max(a1, a2),

readout rd(a,l,u) = u/l and identity (-inf, 0, 0). prop:exact-monoid states that (Sigma, +, 0) is a commutative monoid and that the readout of the fold over any partition is y(q). This file folds left-to-right over key blocks in one pass, which is what a FlashAttention kernel does.

The monoid itself lives in attnbank.components.online_softmax, shared with splitk; this file is only the decision to fold it left-to-right in one pass.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
parameter default block_n 16 sdpa_kernel None

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: This method is exact as built: the conformance suite instantiates it at its default config and requires both y and the weights to match softmax. limit_config() returns {} — the empty dict, not None: there is a limit and no setting has to be changed to reach it.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default sdpa torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention -- on CUDA, FlashAttention-2 or the memory-efficient kernel

Each non-reference entry is a claim that the path is equal to the reference, and tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence checks it on five shapes, both causal settings, float32 and float64. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: lse, n_blocks.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    # Same arithmetic as dense; intermediate storage is one state per query.
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,435,456 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("flash", block_n=16)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = accelerate: the claim is equality with the reference, so that
# is what the example checks.
y_ref = ab.attend("softmax", q, k, v, causal=True)
print("max |y - y_softmax|:", float((out.y - y_ref).abs().max()))

FlashAttention(name='flash', category='exact', objective='accelerate', backend='reference', block_n=16, sdpa_kernel=None)

docs.title: Gated linear attention
docs.text:
gla · ab.build("gla")

Gated linear attention: a data-dependent diagonal gate on the recurrent state.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.GatedLinearAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/gla.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences (row "GLA / Mamba-2"). The operator is

S_t = Diag(alpha_t) S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T,      y_hat_t = S_t^T q_t,
alpha_t = sigmoid(W_alpha x_t)^{1 / tau} in (0, 1)^r,     tau = 16,

the first method in the family whose transition A_t = Diag(alpha_t) depends on the input. Retention can only trade recency against nothing — one rate, chosen in advance, applied to every channel and every token. A data-dependent diagonal gate lets the operator decide per token and per channel what to keep, which is how a fixed r x d_v state stops being a pure recency window and starts being selective. This is the same mechanism Mamba-2's SSD writes as a scalar a_t; GLA keeps it diagonal.

What it does not do is restore the contract. y_hat_t = S_t^T q_t has no denominator — the GroupNorm in the GLA block is not one — and q, k are raw projections with no positive feature map, so the weights

w_{tj} = < q_t , (prod_{u = j+1}^{t} alpha_u) * k_j > / sqrt(d),    j <= t,

are signed and their row sums are whatever the gates and the content make them. That is three of the properties of eq:attention_expectation gone at once (sec:memory-state): normalization invariance, constant preservation and convex-hull confinement. normalize=True restores a measure and is not GLA.

The gate. A trained GLA computes alpha_t from a low-rank projection of the token; with no training there is no W_alpha, so this reference reads the gate off the key itself, alpha_t = sigmoid(k_t)^{1 / tau}. It is a stand-in for the learned map and is stated here rather than hidden: what the library needs from it is that the gate be in (0, 1), data-dependent, and per channel, and all three survive. The 1 / tau exponent is the paper's, and it is load-bearing — it keeps log alpha = logsigmoid(k) / tau close to zero, which is what stops the cumulative product from underflowing over a long prefix. gate_temp=1 turns it off and the state's memory collapses to a few tokens.

The cumulative products are taken in log space by _gated.gated_weights, which is the numerically stable half of the chunked GLA kernel; see that module.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default gate_temp 16.0 gate_bias 0.0 normalize False state_rank None

gate_temp is the paper's tau in alpha = sigmoid(.)^{1/tau}.

gate_bias shifts the gate logits (positive = remember longer). state_rank truncates the key/query dimension and so is the size of the recurrent state, state_rank x d_v; None keeps all d channels.

ab.describe("gla")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: gate, log_gate, mass, state_rank.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.state_rank or d
    return recurrent_cost(m, n, r, dv, bytes_per_el, gate_flops=3)

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,973,824 268,435,456 0.0632× state_bytes 8,192 262,144 0.0312× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("gla", gate_temp=16.0, gate_bias=0.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

GatedLinearAttention(name='gla', category='recurrent', objective='modify', backend='reference', gate_bias=0.0, gate_temp=16.0, normalize=False, state_rank=None)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[gate, log_gate, mass, state_rank], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = False | first row sums: [-0.6341, -1.0423, -1.5651, 1.0365]
extras: ['gate', 'log_gate', 'mass', 'state_rank']

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with gla removed.

changes the same object — recurrent decay_rnn, delta_rnn, hgrn2, hyena, linear_rnn, lru, mega, mlstm, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, recurrent only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, gqa, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, lowrank_ot, mla, otke, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, sinkhorn, unbalanced_sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, modify only
