docs.title: Grouped-query attention
docs.text:
gqa · ab.build("gqa")

Grouped-query attention: K and V shared across groups of query heads.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.GQAAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/gqa.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-arch, sec:exact-roofline. Query heads are partitioned into groups of group_size; the heads of a group share one key–value pair, here obtained by mean-pooling the group's K and V (the conversion recipe of Ainslie et al., 2023). group_size = 1 is multi-head attention, group_size = h is multi-query.

This is an operator modification (tab:comparative: "MQA / GQA / MLA ... mod."), trained as such; measuring it against a multi-head reference answers a conversion question, not an approximation question. Its purpose is the roofline: by eq:exact-decode-intensity the decode arithmetic intensity is (16/b)(h/h_kv), so sharing KV is one of the very few interventions that raises it. cost() divides state_bytes and the KV traffic by group_size accordingly.

Heads are deliberately coupled, so head_independent = False: perturbing head h changes every head in its group and nothing outside it. tests/test_compress.py checks exactly that boundary.

Exact limit: group_size = 1.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent no it shares \(K\)/\(V\) across query heads, so heads are not independent. trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default group_size 2 sdpa_kernel None 
ab.describe("gqa")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with group_size=1 this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("gqa").limit_config
{'group_size': 1}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default sdpa torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention -- on CUDA, FlashAttention-2 or the memory-efficient kernel

Each non-reference entry is a claim that the path is equal to the reference, and tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence checks it on five shapes, both causal settings, float32 and float64. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: group_size, n_kv_heads.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    g = max(1, self.group_size)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el / g,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el / g}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,435,456 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 131,072 262,144 0.5× bytes_moved 393,216 4,718,592 0.0833×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("gqa", group_size=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

GQAAttention(name='gqa', category='compress', objective='modify', backend='reference', group_size=2, sdpa_kernel=None)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=[1, 2, 64, 32], extras=[group_size, n_kv_heads], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
extras: ['group_size', 'n_kv_heads']

docs.title: Hedgehog
docs.text:
hedgehog · ab.build("hedgehog")

Hedgehog: a feature map fitted to the softmax attention it is replacing.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.HedgehogAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/hedgehog.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-det, sec:kernel-limits. Every other entry in this directory picks phi in advance — exp(omega^T u - ||u||^2/2), elu + 1, relu, x^2, 1 + z + z^2/2 — and then asks how close the induced pi_hat lands. Zhang et al. (2024) invert the question: fix the separable form, learn the map. Their diagnosis is that linear attentions fail on two measurable axes, spikiness and monotonicity of the induced weights, and their feature map is built to restore both,

phi_W(u) = softmax([ W u + b ; -(W u + b) ]) in R^{2r},

— an exponential map (spiky) run through a softmax over the feature axis (bounded, so it never overflows), with the negated copy appended so that the map is monotone in <q,k> in both directions. Queries and keys get their own (W, b). The parameters are then obtained by distillation: the paper's Eq. 7 minimises the cross-entropy between the induced measure and the true one,

L = - sum_i sum_j pi_q_i(j) log pi_hat_q_i(j),

which is the KL from softmax to pi_hat up to a constant, so the fit is an explicit projection of softmax onto the rank-2r separable family.

This file performs that projection inside the forward pass, per (batch, head), on the tensors it is given, with Adam in float64 from a seeded initialization. It is therefore an oracle in the sense of nmf_oracle and svd_oracle: it reports how well the best feature map of width 2r that this objective can find does, which upper-bounds what a deployed Hedgehog achieves after distillation on a corpus. Two consequences are declared rather than hidden. trainable = True — the defaults are not a method, they are an initialization plus a fitting budget. And supports_causal = False: the fitted W depends on the whole attention matrix, so an early query's output would move when a later key changed. A deployed Hedgehog distills once and then runs causally; this one cannot, and saying so is cheaper than a mask that does not mean what it says.

The anchor is convergence_configs over steps. More optimization lowers the cross-entropy, which lowers the KL, which lowers the output error — monotonically in the mean, and towards softmax, which no finite budget reaches because the family has rank 2r. steps = 0 is the untrained random feature map and is the worst point of the sequence by construction.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.text:
Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = 2 * (self.r or d)
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 67,108,864 268,435,456 0.25× state_bytes 16,640 262,144 0.0635× bytes_moved 540,928 4,718,592 0.115×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: HGRN2
docs.text:
hgrn2 · ab.build("hgrn2")

HGRN2: a gated vector recurrence expanded to a matrix state by an outer product.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.HGRN2Attention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/hgrn2.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. HGRN is an element-wise gated RNN,

h_t = f_t * h_{t-1} + (1 - f_t) * i_t,                     h_t in R^d,

whose state is a vector: prop:memory-rank caps what it can recall at d numbers however wide the layer is. HGRN2 changes one symbol — the element-wise product becomes an outer product —

H_t = Diag(f_t) H_{t-1} + (1 - f_t) v_t^T,                 H_t in R^{d x d_v},
y_hat_t = H_t^T q_t,

and the state becomes a matrix of d x d_v numbers at exactly the same parameter count. In the vocabulary of this category that is GLA with the key tied to the gate, k_t = 1 - f_t and alpha_t = f_t: HGRN2 has no separate key projection at all, which is the point — the expansion is free.

Two consequences worth stating, because they are what distinguishes this row from GLA.

Per channel the write is a convex combination. Summing the unrolled recurrence channel by channel, sum_{j <= t} (1 - f_j) prod_{u > j} f_u = 1 - prod_{u <= t} f_u <= 1. So the state cannot grow without bound in t, and the weights

w_{tj} = sum_r q_{t,r} (1 - f_{j,r}) prod_{u = j+1}^{t} f_{u,r}

have row sum <q_t, 1 - prod_{u <= t} f_u> — bounded, readable, and equal to one only by accident. Boundedness without normalization again (sec:memory-state); the rows are not a probability measure and the operator declares row_stochastic = False.

The lower bound is where "hierarchical" lives. HGRN sets f_t = gamma + (1 - gamma) sigmoid(.) and makes gamma increase monotonically with depth (via cumax over layers), so lower layers forget fast and model local structure while upper layers approach f = 1 and carry long-range state. A single operator cannot be hierarchical on its own; lower_bound= is that layer's gamma, and sweeping it from 0 to 1 traces the depth axis of the real model. At lower_bound=1 the gate is stuck open, nothing is ever written (1 - f = 0) and the output is exactly zero — the degenerate end of the schedule, reported rather than clamped away.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default lower_bound 0.9 gate_bias 0.0 normalize False state_rank None

lower_bound: this layer's gamma in f = gamma + (1 - gamma) sigmoid.

It is the hierarchical schedule's one free number — 0 at the bottom of the stack, approaching 1 at the top; the default sits mid-stack, because at 0 the untrained gate averages one half and the state keeps barely a token. state_rank truncates the gate/key dimension and so is the size of the recurrent state, state_rank x d_v.

docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Hyena
docs.text:
hyena · ab.build("hyena")

Hyena: implicitly parametrised long convolutions interleaved with gating.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.HyenaAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/hyena.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state. The Hyena operator of order N alternates a long causal convolution with an elementwise ("data-controlled") gate:

z^1 = x^1,     z^{i+1} = x^{i+1} * (h^i conv z^i),     y = z^{N+1},

where x^1 ... x^{N+1} are projections of the input and h^1 ... h^N are filters as long as the sequence. The filters are not stored as n free numbers per channel: they are implicit, the output of a small network applied to a positional encoding of the lag, multiplied by an exponential decay window and normalised. That is what makes a filter of unbounded length a bounded number of parameters, and it is the idea Hyena inherits from continuous-kernel convolutions (Romero et al., 2021).

The claim this file is here to test, and the caveat. h^i depends on the lag alone — it is fixed before any token is seen — so Hyena's convolutional branch has input-independent dynamics exactly like S4, S5 and the LRU. Its gating does not: x^{i+1} is a projection of the input, and multiplying by it makes the composite operator depend on the content at the output position. Hyena is therefore a genuine member of this family in its filters and a partial exception in its gates, which is precisely the distinction sec:memory-state draws when it says the step that produced the current generation of models was to make the state dynamics themselves input-dependent. Hyena moves the data dependence into a pointwise product sitting outside the recurrence; Mamba and the gated linear RNNs move it inside.

No finite state. Unlike every other method in recurrent/, Hyena's filter is not realised by a finite-dimensional recurrence: an arbitrary length-n FIR filter needs O(n) memory to run causally, which is why cost()['state_bytes'] grows with n here and does not for s4d, s5 or lru. prop:memory-rank has nothing to bound. The parameters are few; the state is not.

It does not read the queries or the keys. As in the rest of the family, the three projections are taken from the value field — fixed seeded d_v x d_v matrices, the stand-ins for the learned ones — because a long convolution has nowhere for q and k to enter. extras['reads_qk'] is False.

Weights. expresses_weights = False, twice over: each channel is convolved with its own filter, and the gate multiplies channel by channel, so the output is not sum_j w_{tj} v_j for any scalar w — it is not even linear in v.

Simplifications. The implicit filter here is a two-hidden-layer MLP with sine activations on the positional features [t, sin(2 pi f t), cos(2 pi f t)], windowed by exp(-alpha_c t) with alpha_c log-spaced across channels and L1-normalised, which is the published recipe's shape but not its exact schedule; the short depthwise convolution Hyena applies to the projections before the recurrence is omitted. As everywhere in recurrent/ the convolution is evaluated directly rather than by FFT, so that causality is bit-exact (see s4d).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights no it cannot name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original positions and is excluded from the error decomposition by declaration. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default order 2 width 16 n_freqs 4 decay_min 0.5 decay_max 8.0 seed 0

order: how many (convolution, gate) stages; 2 is the paper's default.

width and n_freqs size the implicit filter network — the hidden width and the number of Fourier features in the positional encoding of the lag — and decay_min / decay_max bound the log-spaced exponential window, which is what sets the effective filter length per channel.

ab.describe("hyena")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: filter_length, filters, order, reads_qk.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """``state_bytes`` grows with ``n``: a long convolution has no finite state."""
    logn = max(1.0, math.log2(max(n, 2)))
    return {"flops": self.order * (15 * dv * n * logn + 2 * n * dv * dv)
            + 2 * n * dv * dv,
            "state_bytes": (self.order + 1) * n * dv * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (n * dv + m * dv
                            + self.order * n * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 44,826,624 268,435,456 0.167× state_bytes 393,216 262,144 1.5× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("hyena", order=2, width=16)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("expresses_weights =", attn.expresses_weights,
      "-- no measure over the original positions exists,",
      "so weights is", out.weights)
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: HyperAttention
docs.text:
hyperattention · ab.build("hyperattention")

HyperAttention: a hashed heavy block plus an unbiased uniform estimate of the rest.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.HyperAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/hyperattention.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-content, and the boundary sec:sparse-content draws between restricting and estimating. HyperAttention splits the row of pi_q in two and treats the halves differently:

  1. Heavy part. sortLSH hashes queries and keys, sorts by bucket, and keeps a contiguous block of block keys per query — a mask H_q that, after the permutation, is block diagonal and so can be run by a dense kernel. These entries are kept exactly.
  2. Light part. The remaining visible keys are sampled uniformly at inclusion probability u = min(1, n_sampled / |S_q^c|) and reweighted by 1/u.

The implied measure is therefore neither a restriction nor a pure importance sample:

w_j = pi_j                   j in H_q,
w_j = pi_j / u               j sampled outside H_q,
pi_hat = w / sum_i w_i.

Numerator and denominator of the residual are unbiased, so the only systematic error is the O(1/n_sampled) self-normalization bias of prop:error-ratio-est, and the hashed block is what keeps the variance of the residual small: the keys whose pi_j / u is large are the ones the hash was meant to catch. The contrast with topk — which simply discards the tail and absorbs eps_q into the head — and with lsh_sample — which samples everything — is the point of having all three.

Scope of the paper's guarantee. Han et al. prove a spectral-norm bound on the approximate attention under two conditions on the matrix (a bounded ratio of column norms, kappa, and a bounded max column l_1 mass), together with their specific sampling scheme. Nothing here re-derives or checks that bound; this file implements the estimator, and the only error statement it makes is the one extras lets you verify numerically.

Deviations from the paper, stated rather than hidden:

  • The paper sorts queries and keys independently by bucket and takes the block diagonal of the permuted m x n matrix, which pairs a query with keys at the same rank quantile. This file places the query at its own bucket's position in the sorted key order and takes the block keys around it. The two agree when queries and keys have the same bucket distribution; pairing by bucket value is what remains well defined for m != n and under causal masking, where the sorted key order is the order of the visible prefix and therefore differs per query. That restriction to the prefix is also what makes the support causal: a key after the query can neither enter the block nor move another key into it.
  • The paper handles causal masking by a recursive decomposition into two halves plus a diagonal block, for which it can reuse the same subroutine. The prefix formulation above is a different route to the same requirement and is not that algorithm.
  • Uniform column sampling is done here as independent per-row Bernoulli draws rather than as one shared column subset, so each row's estimator is unbiased on its own.

Exact limit: n_sampled = None sets u = 1 on the whole complement, so every visible key carries its exact weight and pi_hat = pi — independent of the hash, which is what makes it a test of the reweighting rather than of the mask.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default block 4 n_sampled 4 n_buckets 8 seed 0 hash_seed 0

hash_seed draws the sortLSH rotation and seed the uniform sample.

They are separate generators so that either randomization can be held fixed while the other varies — which is what makes the residual estimator's bias and variance measurable at a fixed mask.

ab.describe("hyperattention")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_sampled=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("hyperattention").limit_config
{'n_sampled': None}

Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

>>> ab.get_class("hyperattention").convergence_configs()
[{'n_sampled': 1}, {'n_sampled': 2}, {'n_sampled': 4}, {'n_sampled': 8}]

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: eps, heavy, heavy_mass, k_realized, n_sampled_realized, support, u.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    half = max(1, self.n_buckets // 2)
    kept = self.block + (self.n_sampled if self.n_sampled is not None else n)
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * d * half + 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 3,145,728 268,435,456 0.0117× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 2,490,368 4,718,592 0.528×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("hyperattention", block=4, n_sampled=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["hyperattention"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"hyperattention": {'block': 4, 'n_sampled': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

HyperAttention(name='hyperattention', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', block=4, hash_seed=0, n_buckets=8, n_sampled=4, seed=0)

docs.title: ISAB
docs.text:
isab · ab.build("isab")

ISAB: the Set Transformer's induced set attention block — a nonlinear bottleneck.

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.ISABAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/isab.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-methods. ISAB routes attention through r learned inducing points I in two multihead attention blocks (Lee et al., 2019):

ISAB(X) = MAB(X, H),      H = MAB(I, X) in R^{r x d},
MAB(X, Y) = LayerNorm( O + rFF(O) ),   O = LayerNorm( X + Attn(X, Y, Y) ).

Written with this library's arguments, the context is (k, v) and the first block summarizes it into r induced rows, the second lets the queries read them:

b(z, x) = softmax_x( beta <i_z, k_x> ),   H = MAB-wrap( I_v + int v db(z, .) ),
a(q, z) = softmax_z( beta <q, (H P)_z> ), y_hat(q) = MAB-wrap( q P_q + a(q, .) H ).

The two attention maps are Markov kernels, but ISAB is not a stochastic factorization and this method declares expresses_weights = False. Three separate things break the composition, and each one alone is enough:

  1. MAB applies a residual, a layer norm and a row-wise feedforward between the hops, so H is a nonlinear function of the values — there is no matrix B with H = B V;
  2. the second block's keys are a projection of H, so even the read kernel depends on the values;
  3. the query-side residual q P_q puts mass on a term that does not come from the value field at all — with a constant value field the output is not that constant, which no probability measure on the n positions can do.

So y is not even linear in V: y(2V) != 2 y(V), and no weight matrix exists to report. This is the contrast sec:factor draws against latent_stochastic, which cites the same paper for the bare two-hop kernel — strip MAB down to its attention and ISAB becomes a stochastic factorization; keep the block that the Set Transformer actually uses and the measure on the original positions is gone. Both kernels are still exposed in extras, as attention maps rather than factors.

objective = MODIFY: ISAB is a set-encoder architecture with a parameter-count and O(r n) cost argument, not an estimator of dense attention, and no r makes it softmax. Both anchors are None and the suite asserts the exemption.

Untrained behaviour (trainable = True): the inducing points I_q, I_v, the two feedforwards and the two projections are seeded Gaussians scaled by 1/sqrt(fan_in); layer norms are parameter-free. The projections P and P_q exist because this library allows d != dv while a Set Transformer is uniformly d_model wide; with d == dv they are the block's own W_K and the identity residual, randomly initialized.

Not causal: the inducing points pool the whole context.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights no it cannot name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original positions and is excluded from the error decomposition by declaration. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r, hid = self.r, max(1, self.width * dv)
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * (d + dv) + 2 * m * r * (d + dv)
                     + 4 * (r + m) * dv * hid + 2 * r * dv * d + 2 * m * d * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * dv * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 46,465,024 268,435,456 0.173× state_bytes 1,024 262,144 0.00391× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: KIVI
docs.text:
kivi · ab.build("kivi")

KIVI: keys quantized per channel, values per token, with a full-precision residual.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.KIVIAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/kivi.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-quant and prop:compress-sensitivity. KIVI is the scheme that reads the key/value asymmetry off the operator and groups the two caches along different axes:

  • Keys, per channel. The scale and zero-point are shared by group consecutive tokens of one channel, so an outlier channel's coarse step stays inside that channel. What matters for pi_q is only the token-varying part of delta l_j = beta <q, delta k_j> — a channel-constant error is absorbed by the softmax normalizer — and per-channel grouping is exactly the choice that makes the surviving part small.
  • Values, per token. y = sum_j pi_j v_j is a weighted average over tokens, so a per-token scale confines each token's representation error to its own summand; no token can poison another.

The residual window is what makes per-channel grouping causal. A per-channel scale pools statistics over tokens, which is why quantkv(axis='channel') refuses causal=True. KIVI avoids this by streaming: the last residual tokens are kept in full precision, and a group of group tokens is quantized only once it is complete and has fallen out of the residual window. A query at absolute position p therefore sees quantized keys only for the groups entirely contained in [0, p + 1 - residual), and full-precision keys for everything more recent: L(p) = group * max(0, (p + 1 - residual) // group) k_hat_j(p) = Q_channel(k)_j if j < L(p), else k_j

The key representation is thus query-dependent, which is the honest rendering of a streaming cache; the score matrix is assembled by selecting between the two score matrices rather than by materialising [m, n, d] keys. Nothing before position t can depend on a token at or after t, which is what the conformance suite checks.

Values need no residual: per-token quantization is already causal, and Invariant W requires a single v_hat per position, so the value residual of Algorithm 1 is dropped here and recorded as such.

Quantize–dequantize is simulated in the input dtype (via attnbank.components.quantization.affine_quantize). The error is real; the memory saving is not — cost() reports what the scheme would store, including the per-group scale and zero-point, which is the term that stops group from shrinking to one.

Exact limit: bits_k = bits_v = None (the identity quantizer). Affine quantization at 16 bits is not bit-exact in fp32, so it would be a dishonest anchor.

Paper defaults are group = 32 and residual = 128; the defaults here are scaled to the bank's test sizes so that the default configuration actually quantizes something.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """Quantized groups, the full-precision residual, and the scales both need."""
    res = min(self.residual, n)
    nq = (max(0, n - res) // self.group) * self.group
    nf = n - nq
    bk = (self.bits_k or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    bv = (self.bits_v or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    # per-channel key scales: 2 per (group, channel); per-token value scales: 2 each
    scales = 2 * bytes_per_el * (-(-nq // self.group) * d + nq)
    state = nq * (d * bk + dv * bv) + nf * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + scales
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + n * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": state,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + state}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,566,528 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 71,136 262,144 0.271× bytes_moved 333,280 4,718,592 0.0706×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: KVQuant
docs.text:
kvquant · ab.build("kvquant")

KVQuant: pre-RoPE per-channel keys, a sensitivity-weighted non-uniform datatype, and isolated outliers.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.KVQuantAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/kvquant.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-quant and prop:compress-sensitivity. Where kivi changes only the grouping axis, KVQuant changes the coordinate system, the datatype and the support of the quantizer, in four independent moves that this file exposes as four switches:

  1. Per-channel keys (bits_k). The scale and zero-point are shared by all tokens of one channel, which is where the key outliers live. Values stay per token, because y averages over tokens.
  2. Pre-RoPE (pre_rope). RoPE rotates channel pairs by a position-dependent angle, so after it the "outlier channel" structure that per-channel grouping exploits is smeared across each pair. KVQuant stores the key before the rotation and re-applies RoPE on the fly after dequantization. The bank's tensors are post-RoPE by convention, so this file un-rotates, quantizes, and re-rotates — the same three operations the cache performs, in the same order.
  3. Non-uniform datatype (nuq). The quantization signposts are the centroids of a sensitivity-weighted k-means on the entries of each vector, minimising sum_i F_i (x_i - Q(x_i))^2 rather than the unweighted error a uniform grid minimises. KVQuant takes F from the diagonal Fisher information of the language model on a calibration set. No such gradient exists inside a single attention block, so the bank uses the exact local sensitivity instead, which is the first-order term of eq:error-joint: F[j, c] = sum_i (beta pi_ij)^2 ||v_j - y_i||^2 q_ic^2

This is the same objective with the same role for F; it is a different (and, for one layer in isolation, sharper) estimate of it. Under pre_rope the weight is averaged within each RoPE channel pair, which makes it invariant to the rotation it has to survive. For values the local sensitivity is sum_i pi_ij^2, constant along the channel axis, so sensitivity weighting is provably a no-op for a per-token value quantizer and is not applied — a small result worth stating rather than hiding behind a flag. 4. Dense-and-sparse (sparsity). A per-vector fraction of numerical outliers is held in full precision and excluded from the range, so the remaining levels are spent on the dense part. Thresholds are per vector: per channel for the keys, per token for the values, as in the paper. keep_first additionally pins the first token exactly — the attention sink, which carries disproportionate mass and whose value error is therefore not averaged away.

Not causal. A per-channel scale, an outlier threshold and a codebook are all statistics over tokens. KVQuant computes them offline on a calibration set, which makes them constants at serving time; the bank has no calibration set and derives them from the sequence itself, which is a genuinely non-causal operation. Declaring supports_causal = False records that rather than hiding it behind a mask. kivi is the member of this family that is causal, and the residual window is what it pays.

Quantize–dequantize is simulated in the input dtype; no memory is actually saved. cost() reports what the scheme would store, including the per-channel scales, the codebook and the fp16 outliers — the three overheads that decide whether 2 bits is 2 bits.

Exact limit: bits_k = bits_v = None. The RoPE round trip is then skipped entirely, so the limit is exact and not merely accurate.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with bits_k=None, bits_v=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("kvquant").limit_config
{'bits_k': None, 'bits_v': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It returns both the exact and the perturbed score matrices (s, s_hat) in extras — the perturbation is the object of study, and a fused kernel hands back neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: delta_k, delta_v, s, s_hat, sensitivity.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """Payload, per-channel/per-token scales, the NUQ codebook and the fp16 outliers."""
    bk = (self.bits_k or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    bv = (self.bits_v or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    book = 0.0
    if self.nuq:                                   # one codebook per quantized vector
        book = bytes_per_el * ((2 ** (self.bits_k or 4)) * d
                               + (2 ** (self.bits_v or 4)) * n)
    scales = 0.0 if self.nuq else 2 * bytes_per_el * (d + n)
    sparse = 2 * self.sparsity * (n * d + n * dv) * (bytes_per_el + 2)
    pinned = self.keep_first * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el
    state = n * (d * bk + dv * bv) + book + scales + sparse + pinned
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + self.iters * n * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": state,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + state}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 269,484,032 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 77,302 262,144 0.295× bytes_moved 339,446 4,718,592 0.0719×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("kvquant", bits_k=3, bits_v=3)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["kvquant"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"kvquant": {'bits_k': 3, 'bits_v': 3}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

KVQuantAttention(name='kvquant', category='compress', objective='approximate', backend='reference', bits_k=3, bits_v=3, iters=8, keep_first=1, nuq=True, pre_rope=True, sensitivity=True, sparsity=0.01, theta=10000.0)

docs.title: Latent stochastic factorization
docs.text:
latent_stochastic · ab.build("latent_stochastic")

Latent stochastic factorization: two Markov kernels through r latents.

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LatentStochasticAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/latent_stochastic.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-def, def:factor-stochastic, prop:factor-closure. A rank-r latent stochastic factorization is a pair of Markov kernels a: Q -> Z (read) and b: Z -> X (write) with

pi_hat_q(dx) = sum_z a(q, z) b(z, dx),    P_hat = A B,
A in R_{>=0}^{m x r} with A 1 = 1,   B in R_{>=0}^{r x n} with B 1 = 1.

Both kernels are attentions (eq:factor-write, eq:factor-read):

b(z, .) = softmax_x( beta <w_z, k_x> ),     w_z a latent query,
a(q, z) = softmax_z( beta <q, kbar_z> ),    kbar_z = int k_x b(z, dx),

the ABC form in which the latent keys summarize the context rather than being free (Peng et al., 2022). The latent queries w_z are the learned parameters; here they are a seeded Gaussian, so trainable = True records that the method is only meaningful after training.

prop:factor-closure is why this category exists separately from low-rank approximation: a composition of Markov kernels is automatically a probability measure, so normalization, constant preservation and convex-hull confinement all survive — none of which holds for a generic signed rank-r factorization. The output has the two-level form y_hat(q) = sum_z a(q,z) u(z) with u(z) = int v db(z,.), so the context is seen only through r latent values.

This is an operator modification (tab:comparative): there is no r at which it becomes softmax, and nothing it converges to, so both correctness anchors are None by design. It loses fs (full support in the exact sense) and ql.

Not causal: the write kernel pools over the whole context.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default r 8 seed 0 
ab.describe("latent_stochastic")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The measure is a product \(a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\) — an SVD, an NMF, a clustering, a pair of small softmaxes — and sdpa computes one softmax, not a product of two.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: a, b, latent_keys, latent_values, r.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.r
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * (d + dv) + 2 * m * r * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 4,194,304 268,435,456 0.0156× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 264,192 4,718,592 0.056×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("latent_stochastic", r=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: Latte
docs.text:
latte · ab.build("latte")

Latte: latent attention as a probabilistic model — the free latent space.

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LatteAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/latte.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-def, def:factor-stochastic. Latte (Dolga et al., 2024) introduces a latent variable l with r states that renders query and context conditionally independent, x ⊥ q | l, and reads the attention measure straight off the factorization

pi_hat_q(x) = sum_l p(x | l) p(l | q),      Latte(Q, K, V) = softmax_r(Q) softmax_n(K)^T V,

with the two conditionals parameterized by one latent array each:

p(l | q) = softmax_l( beta <q, w^q_l> ),    normalized over the r LATENTS,
p(x | l) = softmax_x( beta <k_x, w^k_l> ),  normalized over the n POSITIONS.

Both factors are Markov kernels, so this is a stochastic factorization in the sense of def:factor-stochastic, weights is their product and prop:factor-closure applies unchanged.

What separates it from latent_stochastic / abc is where the latent keys come from. There the read kernel is softmax_z(beta <q, k_bar_z>) with k_bar_z = int k db(z, .) summarizing the context; here w^q_l is free, so

the read kernel a(q, .) does not look at the context at all.

The query's only interaction with the keys is through which of r latents it selects: pi_hat has rank at most r, and perturbing every key and value leaves a bit-for-bit unchanged. That is the cleanest instance in the bank of a factorization whose two hops are genuinely separate — and the reason it is an operator modification: no setting of r recovers softmax, because the free latents never see the keys. Both anchors are None by design (tab:comparative, "mod.").

Causal (Latte's autoregressive form): the write kernel is normalized over the prefix, p(x | l, t) = softmax_{x <= t}(beta <k_x, w^k_l>), which the paper computes with cumulative sums; the read kernel is untouched, since it never depended on the context. This reference implementation materializes the prefix-normalized kernel [m, r, n] and softmaxes each prefix independently — clarity over speed, and stable at any logit scale.

The latent arrays w^q, w^k are the learned parameters; untrained they are seeded Gaussians, so trainable = True. Scaling: the paper writes the logits unscaled; here they carry the bank's beta = 1/sqrt(d) so that the two kernels are on the same footing as every other method's.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default r 8 seed 0

r: number of latent states. There is no r at which this is softmax.

ab.describe("latte")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The measure is a product \(a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\) — an SVD, an NMF, a clustering, a pair of small softmaxes — and sdpa computes one softmax, not a product of two.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: a, b, latent_keys, latent_queries, latent_values, r.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.r
    return {"flops": 2 * m * r * d + 2 * n * r * (d + dv) + 2 * m * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 4,194,304 268,435,456 0.0156× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("latte", r=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])

docs.title: Linear transformer
docs.text:
linear_elu · ab.build("linear_elu")

Linear transformer: the fixed feature map phi(u) = elu(u) + 1.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LinearELUAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/linear_elu.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-det. Katharopoulos et al. (2020) replace the interaction by

g_hat(q, x) = <phi(q), phi(k_x)>,   phi(u) = elu(u) + 1 > 0,   r = d,

with no resource parameter, so <phi(q), phi(k)> -> exp(beta <q,k>) holds in no sense: this is an operator modification, not an approximation (def:kernel-regimes, tab:kernel-methods row "Linear transformer ... no"). The library records that by objective = modify and by returning None from both correctness anchors: there is no configuration under which it becomes softmax, and nothing it converges to.

Because phi > 0 the induced measure is a genuine probability measure, so this is one of the normalized members of the family; lem:kernel-mixture then says pi_hat_q is a mixture of r = d query-independent context distributions, and prop:kernel-retrieval bounds what it can retrieve. rem:kernel-homogeneous applies approximately: for large positive coordinates phi is linear, so the query norm cannot sharpen pi_hat_q.

The normalized form of eq:kernel-moments is used (divide by phi(q)^T z). Many deployed descendants drop the denominator and normalize the output instead (sec:memory-state); that variant lives in recurrent/linear_rnn.py, where the loss of normalization invariance is the point.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This method takes no configuration of its own — only the base class's scale and backend.

ab.describe("linear_elu")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: Z_hat, g_hat.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = d
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv + (m + n) * r,
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,908,288 268,435,456 0.063× state_bytes 8,320 262,144 0.0317× bytes_moved 532,608 4,718,592 0.113×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("linear_elu")
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: Linear attention as a recurrence
docs.text:
linear_rnn · ab.build("linear_rnn")

Linear attention as a recurrence: H_t = H_{t-1} + psi(k_t) v_t^T.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LinearRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/linear_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, prop:memory-suff, prop:memory-rank. A separable interaction of rank r admits a sufficient statistic of size r x d_v: the prefix moments H_t = sum_{i<=t} psi(k_i) v_i^T (and z_t = sum psi(k_i)) are all a future query needs. prop:memory-rank is the converse: an additive finite-state memory forces the interaction to have finite rank, so recall is bounded by the state.

With the normalizer kept this is linear_elu. The deployed form, and the one here, drops it (readout = H_t^T phi(q_t)) because the denominator can approach zero and produce unbounded gradients. Three properties of eq:attention_expectation go with it (sec:memory-state): normalization invariance under g -> c(q) g, constant preservation (y_hat = c <phi(q), z> now scales with context length), and the convex-hull bound. Set normalize=True to put the denominator back and watch all three return.

The weights on the original positions are w_{tj} = <phi(q_t), psi(k_j)> for j <= t: nonnegative for a positive feature map, but not summing to one. Invariant W still holds exactly, which is why this category is in the library at all.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: mass, state_rank.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = d
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * dv * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,777,216 268,435,456 0.0625× state_bytes 8,192 262,144 0.0312× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("linear_rnn", feature='elu', normalize=False)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with linear_rnn removed.

changes the same object — recurrent decay_rnn, delta_rnn, gla, hgrn2, hyena, lru, mega, mlstm, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, recurrent only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, gqa, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, lowrank_ot, mla, otke, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, sinkhorn, unbalanced_sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, modify only

Open the browser with linear_rnn selected and tick up to three more to see them in columns. Every row there is one the registry declares, and the rows the selected methods agree on fold away.

docs.title: Linformer
docs.text:
linformer · ab.build("linformer")

Linformer: a fixed linear projection of K and V along the sequence axis.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LinformerAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/linformer.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-lowrank, sec:factor-methods. With E, F in R^{r x n},

P_hat = softmax(beta Q (E K)^T) in R^{m x r},    y_hat = P_hat (F V),

so E K and F V are r learned pseudo-tokens: the method compresses keys and values separately, changes both mu and v, fixes n, and is not causal.

It can be written on the original positions, and that is how the library stores it: y_hat = (P_hat F) V, so weights = P_hat F in R^{m x n} with the original values. Those weights are generally signed and their rows do not sum to one unless F is row-stochastic, which is the paper's point — tab:comparative lists Linformer as losing nm and hl. row_stochastic = False records it, and the row sums are returned in extras so the deviation can be measured.

Note also that the latent keys (EK)_z enter the softmax linearly, and exp(beta <q, sum_x E_zx k_x>) != sum_x E_zx exp(beta <q, k_x>), so the entries of P are not approximated at all; the Johnson–Lindenstrauss argument is an existence statement about the reference operator with random E, F, not an error bound for the trained operator.

Exact limit: r = None sets E = F = I_n, which gives dense softmax.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:

{'r': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The compressed context is built by this method, and the measure it reports lives on the original \(n\) positions — a kernel run over the compressed cache would return neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: latent_weights, r, row_sum.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = min(self.r or n, n)
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * (d + dv) + 2 * m * r * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 4,194,304 268,435,456 0.0156× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 264,192 4,718,592 0.056×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("linformer", r=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["linformer"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"linformer": {'r': 8}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})
