docs.title: Longformer
docs.text:
longformer · ab.build("longformer")

Longformer: a dilated sliding window plus task-global tokens.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LongformerAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/longformer.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-fixed. Longformer's support is the union of three query-independent pieces (Beltagy et al., 2020, Sec. 3):

  • sliding window — "given a fixed window size w, each token attends to w/2 tokens on each side";
  • dilated sliding window — the window is given "gaps of size dilation d", so l stacked layers reach l * d * w. The paper uses different dilations on different heads, "allowing some heads without dilation to focus on local context, while others with dilation focus on longer context"; head_dilation=True reproduces that;
  • global attention — "a token with a global attention attends to all tokens across the sequence, and all tokens in the sequence attend to it". The pattern is therefore not symmetric in the two directions of the restriction: a global position widens every row, and its own row is dense.

Written in the paper's notation, query p keeps

S_p = { p + i*d : -w/2 <= i <= w/2 }  u  { 0, ..., n_global - 1 },

and S_p is the whole visible row when p < n_global. Offset i = 0 is always present, so no row is ever empty; the support is then intersected with the causal mask, which both removes the right half of the window (Longformer's own autoregressive configuration) and makes the global prefix behave like the sinks of sink_window — except that the global rows stay dense, which is the whole difference between a sink and a global token.

The error is purely distributional: y - y_hat = eps_p (m_{S^c} - m_S) (prop:sparse-identity), with eps_p returned in extras.

Dilation alone (w=None, dilation=d) is the pure "strided column" pattern that LongNet later scales up with exponentially growing dilation rates.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default w 8 dilation 1 n_global 0 head_dilation False

w: Longformer's window size — w//2 per side (None = unbounded).

dilation: gap between attended positions. head_dilation: give head h the dilation 1 + (h % dilation), so head 0 stays local while later heads reach further — Longformer's per-head configuration. n_global: the number of leading positions that are globally attended and attend globally.

docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    kept = min(n, (self.w + 1 if self.w is not None else n) + self.n_global)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": kept * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

docs.title: Low-precision attention
docs.text:
lowprec · ab.build("lowprec")

Low-precision attention: simulated FP8 / INT8 logits and values.

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LowPrecisionAttention, attnbank/methods/exact/lowprec.py monograph sec:exact-boundary

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:exact-boundary. This is the method that marks where exactness ends. An FP8/INT8 kernel keeps the evaluation order of prop:exact-monoid but stores the operands at a precision u' >> u, so it satisfies the first clause of def:exact-scheme and fails the second. By the criterion of "which object is changed" it belongs with context compression: quantizing q, k replaces g by g_hat (a distributional error) and quantizing v or P replaces v by v_hat (a value-representation error). Its objective is therefore approximate, not accelerate, which is the whole point of putting it in exact/.

Simulation is quantize–dequantize in the kernel, per attention head and per tensor:

Q_b(x) = clamp(round(x / Delta), -2^{b-1}, 2^{b-1} - 1) * Delta,  Delta = max|x| / (2^{b-1} - 1)

for signed INT-b, and round-to-nearest on the FP8 E4M3 / E5M2 grids. Optional incoherent processing (hadamard=True) multiplies q and k by a shared random orthogonal Hadamard matrix before quantizing, which is exact in infinite precision (<Rq, Rk> = <q, k>) and spreads outlier coordinates, as in FlashAttention-3's FP8 path. Optional smoothing (smooth_k=True) subtracts the token mean of k, which shifts every logit of a query by one constant and so leaves pi_q exactly invariant (SageAttention).

The quantizers themselves live in attnbank.components.quantization, shared with quantkv: one implementation, one place where the rounding rule is argued about.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default bits 8 fmt None bits_p None hadamard_qk False smooth_k False seed 0

bits: INT width for q, k, v (None = no quantization, the exact limit). fmt: 'e4m3' / 'e5m2' to use FP8 instead of INT. bits_p: optional INT width for the attention weights themselves.

ab.describe("lowprec")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with bits=None, fmt=None, bits_p=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("lowprec").limit_config
{'bits': None, 'fmt': None, 'bits_p': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The method exists to expose the intermediate states of the evaluation, which a single fused call does not hand back.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: delta_v, s_hat.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = bytes_per_el if self.bits is None and self.fmt is None else \
        max(1, (8 if self.fmt else self.bits) // 8)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv), "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * b,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * b}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,435,456 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 131,072 262,144 0.5× bytes_moved 262,144 4,718,592 0.0556×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lowprec", bits=8, hadamard_qk=False)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["lowprec"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"lowprec": {'bits': 8, 'hadamard_qk': False}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

LowPrecisionAttention(name='lowprec', category='exact', objective='approximate', backend='reference', bits=8, bits_p=None, fmt=None, hadamard_qk=False, seed=0, smooth_k=False)

docs.title: Hidden-dimension low rank
docs.text:
lowrank_kv · ab.build("lowrank_kv")

Hidden-dimension low rank: truncated SVD of the key and value channel matrices.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LowRankKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/lowrank_kv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-lowrank. With Pi_r an orthogonal projector of rank r on the channel space,

k_hat_j = Pi_r^K k_j,   v_hat_j = Pi_r^V v_j,

where Pi_r^K and Pi_r^V are the leading right singular subspaces of K and V. The two errors are structurally different, which is the point of the file:

  • Keys. delta_l_j = -beta <(I - Pi_r) q, (I - Pi_r) k_j>, so a subspace chosen from the keys alone fails exactly when the queries load on low-variance key directions — no amount of key energy captured says anything until the query is known.
  • Values. Since pi_hat is unaffected by a value projection, the value error is sum_j pi_j (I - Pi_r) v_j = (I - Pi_r) y(q): the projection residual of the output, not of the approximate output and not of the raw value matrix. So the optimal value subspace is the leading eigenspace of the attention-weighted second moment of the outputs.

Not causal: the SVD pools over all tokens. The factorization is computed in float64 so that the exact limit (rank_k = rank_v = None) is exact to machine precision.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default rank_k 4 rank_v 4 
ab.describe("lowrank_kv")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with rank_k=None, rank_v=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("lowrank_kv").limit_config
{'rank_k': None, 'rank_v': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It returns both the exact and the perturbed score matrices (s, s_hat) in extras — the perturbation is the object of study, and a fused kernel hands back neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: basis_k, basis_v, q_residual, s, s_hat.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    rk, rv = min(self.rank_k or d, d), min(self.rank_v or dv, dv)
    state = n * (rk + rv) * bytes_per_el
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * n * (d * rk + dv * rv),
            "state_bytes": state,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + state}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 269,484,032 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 16,384 262,144 0.0625× bytes_moved 278,528 4,718,592 0.059×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lowrank_kv", rank_k=4, rank_v=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["lowrank_kv"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"lowrank_kv": {'rank_k': 4, 'rank_v': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Low-rank logits
docs.text:
lowrank_logit · ab.build("lowrank_logit")

Oracle — an upper bound, not a method

lowrank_logit is not deployable and is not meant to be. It uses information no inference-time method has, and it is in the bank to answer how well could this ever work? — several of the monograph's arguments need that number. Read every result below as a bound on a family of real methods, never as a baseline you could ship.

Low-rank logits: truncate the logits to rank r, then softmax what is left.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LowRankLogitAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/lowrank_logit.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-matrix. Everything else in the bank that says "low rank" is low rank in the wrong space. linformer projects the sequence axis of K and V, svd_oracle truncates P itself, nystrom factors P through landmarks — all three produce a signed measure, because a rank-r approximation of a nonnegative matrix is not nonnegative. This file truncates one step earlier:

S   = beta Q K^T,      S_r = U_r Sigma_r V_r^T   (truncated SVD, float64),
g_hat(q, x) = exp((S_r)_{qx}),   pi_hat = softmax(S_r).

The exponential is applied after the truncation, so pi_hat is a genuine probability measure for every r: nonnegative, unit mass, output inside the convex hull of the values. The whole contract survives, and the error is pure hl — the measure is wrong, but it is still a measure. That is the comparison this file exists to make: at equal rank, is it better to be optimal in P and signed, or suboptimal in P and stochastic? svd_oracle is the other arm.

The rank that matters. S = beta Q K^T already has rank at most d, so the method is exactly softmax for any r >= min(m, n, d) and the truncation only bites below the head dimension — which is exactly Bhojanapalli et al.'s low-rank bottleneck, stated as an operator rather than as an architectural constraint. Note also that rank(S_r) = r says nothing about rank(exp(S_r)): the entrywise exponential of a rank-one matrix is generically full rank, so a low-rank interaction is not a low-rank attention matrix, and this method is not a factorization in the sense of sec:factor.

This is an oracle: it needs the full m x n logit matrix and an SVD of it, so it buys nothing at inference. It exists to bound what a rank-r surrogate of the interaction can achieve, and to separate that bound from the rank of P.

Exact limit: r = None keeps the full spectrum. Not causal: the truncation does not preserve the mask's -inf entries, and an SVD of a matrix containing -inf is not defined.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
parameter default r 4

r: rank kept in the logit matrix; None keeps all of it (the limit).

ab.describe("lowrank_logit")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with r=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("lowrank_logit").limit_config
{'r': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: logit_error, r, singular_values, spectral_energy.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    rmax = min(m, n)
    r = min(self.r or rmax, rmax)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * d + 2 * m * n * rmax + 2 * m * n * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * (m + n) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,415,919,104 268,435,456 9× state_bytes 16,384 262,144 0.0625× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lowrank_logit", r=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["lowrank_logit"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"lowrank_logit": {'r': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: LOTFormer-style factored coupling
docs.text:
lowrank_ot · ab.build("lowrank_ot")

LOTFormer-style factored coupling: transport through r pivots.

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LowRankOTAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/lowrank_ot.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot ("Factorization through a pivot measure"), eq:ot-glued, and eq:factor-pivot. Let rho be a probability measure on r pivots. Given gamma_1 in Pi(nu, rho) and gamma_2 in Pi(rho, mubar), the glued coupling

gamma(dq, dx) = sum_z rho_z gamma_1(dq | z) gamma_2(dx | z)
              = Gamma_1 diag(rho)^{-1} Gamma_2

lies in Pi(nu, mubar), has rank at most r, and has query conditional pi^piv_q = sum_z gamma_1(z | q) gamma_2(. | z). Both halves are solved by Sinkhorn on dot-product costs (queries-to-pivots, pivots-to-keys), so the whole thing costs O((m + n) r) and never forms the m x n matrix.

Two readings of the same object. As a coupling it is doubly stochastic and so balances participation of context positions — no key absorbs the mass of all queries. As a factorization it is exactly def:factor-stochastic: A_{iz} = gamma_1(z|q_i) and B_{zj} = gamma_2(j|z) are both row-stochastic, so prop:factor-closure applies and pi_hat is a probability measure by construction. It is filed under coupling because the column constraint, absent from the row-stochastic factorizations of sec:factor, is the thing it adds.

It is a new operator: a doubly stochastic coupling does not approximate softmax, whose column sums are unconstrained, and it is not claimed to approximate the full plan of prop:ot-conditional either. Hence no exact limit and no convergence sequence — the pivots are learned end to end, so trainable = True.

Not causal, for the reason in prop:ot-causal.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default r 4 n_iter 10 eps 1.0 seed 0 
ab.describe("lowrank_ot")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A fixed-point iteration over the whole matrix is not a kernel call, and the normalisation it computes is not per-query.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: a, b, col_marginal, pivots, r.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.r
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * (m + n) * r * dv
                    + 2 * self.n_iter * (m + n) * r,
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,260,992 268,435,456 0.00842× state_bytes 1,024 262,144 0.00391× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lowrank_ot", r=4, n_iter=10)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

docs.title: LRU
docs.text:
lru · ab.build("lru")

LRU: a diagonal linear RNN with a stable parametrisation, and no state-space theory.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LRUAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/lru.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. The recurrence is exactly S5's,

h_t = lambda * h_{t-1} + gamma * (B v_t),      y_t = Re(C h_t) + D * v_t,

run with the same parallel scan. What is different is where lambda comes from. There is no continuous-time system, no HiPPO matrix and no discretisation step. The eigenvalues are parametrised directly in polar form,

lambda_n = exp(-exp(nu_n) + i exp(theta_n)),

which is stable by construction — |lambda_n| = exp(-exp(nu_n)) < 1 for every real nu_n, so no projection or clipping is ever needed — and initialised with |lambda_n| uniform on a ring [r_min, r_max] and the phase uniform on [0, max_phase]. The input is rescaled by gamma_n = sqrt(1 - |lambda_n|^2), the normalisation that keeps the state's variance O(1) instead of O(1/(1-|lambda|)) however long the memory is.

That is the claim the method is here to make, and it is the reason the library carries s5 and lru side by side rather than one of them: Orvieto et al. show that a linear diagonal recurrence with a careful parametrisation matches deep state-space models on Long Range Arena, so what S4 and S5 contribute is the structure — linear, diagonal, stable, normalised — and not the state-space derivation that motivated it. tests/test_recurrent_ssm.py makes this concrete: one sequential loop reproduces s5 and lru from their own extras, because there is only one recurrence.

Dynamics are input-independent. lambda, gamma, B, C and D are parameters. Nothing in the transition depends on v_t, and the queries and keys are not read at all (extras['reads_qk'] is False); the operator is a matrix-valued convolution in the lag. Letting lambda depend on the token is exactly the step the gated linear RNNs took, and it is the boundary of this family.

Weights. expresses_weights = False, for S5's reason: C lambda^l B is a d_v x d_v matrix per lag, the operator mixes channels as well as positions, and there is no scalar measure over the original positions to report.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights no it cannot name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original positions and is excluded from the error decomposition by declaration. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

parameter default n_state 16 r_min 0.0 r_max 1.0 max_phase 6.283185307179586 feedthrough True seed 0

n_state: the size N of the (channel-shared) complex state.

r_min / r_max bound |lambda| at initialisation — the memory horizon, since mode n decays with time constant -1/log|lambda_n| — and max_phase bounds the initial phase. The defaults are the paper's.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: b_bar, c_eff, d_skip, lam, n_state, radius, reads_qk, state_size.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.n_state
    return {"flops": 8 * n * r * dv + 8 * n * r + 8 * m * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": 2 * r * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (n * dv + m * dv + 4 * r * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,908,288 268,435,456 0.063× state_bytes 64 262,144 0.000244× bytes_moved 270,336 4,718,592 0.0573×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lru", n_state=16, r_min=0.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("expresses_weights =", attn.expresses_weights,
      "-- no measure over the original positions exists,",
      "so weights is", out.weights)
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

LRUAttention(name='lru', category='recurrent', objective='modify', backend='reference', feedthrough=True, max_phase=6.283185307179586, n_state=16, r_max=1.0, r_min=0.0, seed=0)

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with lru removed.

changes the same object — recurrent decay_rnn, delta_rnn, gla, hgrn2, hyena, linear_rnn, mega, mlstm, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, recurrent only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, gqa, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, lowrank_ot, mla, otke, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, sinkhorn, unbalanced_sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, modify only

Open the browser with lru selected and tick up to three more to see them in columns. Every row there is one the registry declares, and the rows the selected methods agree on fold away.

docs.title: LSH importance sampling
docs.text:
lsh_sample · ab.build("lsh_sample")

LSH importance sampling: MagicPIG-style key sampling with unbiased reweighting.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LSHSampleAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/lsh_sample.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-content ("Sampling is not restriction") and prop:error-ratio-est. A key set S is sampled with inclusion probabilities u_j monotone in the attention score, and the output is the self-normalized importance-sampling estimator (eq:sparse-snis)

y_hat(q) = sum_{j in S} (g_j / u_j) v_j  /  sum_{j in S} (g_j / u_j),
pi_hat_j = 1{j in S} (pi_j / u_j) / sum_i 1{i in S} (pi_i / u_i).

Numerator and normalizer are unbiased for N(q) and Z(q); the ratio is only consistent, with O(1/N_s) bias (Owen, 2013). Unlike deterministic restriction this does not systematically reallocate tail mass to the head — it trades the value-dependent bias of prop:sparse-identity for variance, whose size is (1 + chi2(pi || lambda)) / N_s times sup_x ||v(x) - y||^2 (prop:error-ratio-est (b)).

Proposal. MagicPIG derives u_j from SimHash collision probabilities; this reference implementation abstracts that to a tempered proposal lambda_j ∝ exp(alpha * s_j) on the visible keys, with alpha = 0 uniform and alpha = 1 tracking pi exactly, and Poisson (independent Bernoulli) sampling at u_j = min(1, N_s * lambda_j). Sweeping alpha is how chi2(pi || lambda), the quantity the bound is stated in, is varied.

Exact limit. n_samples = None sets u_j = 1 for every visible key, so S is the whole visible context and pi_hat = pi exactly.

Degenerate draw. If a row samples nothing, the single largest-score visible key is inserted so the estimator is defined; the event is counted in extras["empty_draws"].

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_samples 8 alpha 1.0 seed 0 
ab.describe("lsh_sample")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_samples=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("lsh_sample").limit_config
{'n_samples': None}

Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

>>> ab.get_class("lsh_sample").convergence_configs()
[{'n_samples': 2}, {'n_samples': 4}, {'n_samples': 8}, {'n_samples': 14}]

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2_pi_lambda, empty_draws, eps, n_sampled, support, u.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    ns = self.n_samples or n
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * d + 2 * m * ns * dv,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + m * ns * dv + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 135,266,304 268,435,456 0.504× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 1,441,792 4,718,592 0.306×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("lsh_sample", n_samples=8, alpha=1.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["lsh_sample"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"lsh_sample": {'n_samples': 8, 'alpha': 1.0}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Mega
docs.text:
mega · ab.build("mega")

Mega: a multi-dimensional damped EMA in front of chunked gated attention.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.MegaAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/mega.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, sec:sparse. Mega keeps softmax attention but puts a recurrence in front of it. A multi-dimensional damped exponential moving average smooths the sequence before the queries and keys are read off it,

h_t^{(j)} = alpha_j * (beta_j x_{t,j}) + (1 - alpha_j * delta_j) * h_{t-1}^{(j)},
EMA(x)_{t,j} = <eta_j, h_t^{(j)}>,

one ndim-dimensional state per feature j, and the attention that follows is restricted to chunks of c positions so that the cost is linear in the sequence length. In the bank's signature that reads

q' = EMA(q),   k' = EMA(k),   pi_t = softmax_{j in chunk(t), j <= t} (<q'_t, k'_j> / sqrt d),
y_t = sum_j pi_t(j) v_j,

with v left alone — in Mega the values come from the input directly while Q and K are read off the smoothed sequence, which is the whole mechanism: the EMA supplies the local, position-based inductive bias that lets a chunk-local attention still see something about the rest of the sequence.

Input-independent dynamics, with a real caveat. The EMA's coefficients alpha, delta, beta, eta are parameters; the recurrence h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t has A independent of x_t, so the EMA belongs to this family exactly as S4D and the LRU do. The attention branch does not: pi_t is computed from the content of q' and k' and is as input-dependent as any softmax. Mega is thus not an instance of the family's defining restriction taken as a whole — only its recurrent component is — and the operator is a hybrid rather than a pure state-space layer. sec:memory-state records the same caveat about the headline model's cost: full gated attention plus an EMA is quadratic, and only the chunked variant implemented here (chunk not None) is linear.

Weights. Unlike the rest of this family, Mega does express a measure on the original n positions, and a row-stochastic one: the chunk-restricted softmax. The EMA changes which positions get the mass, not whether the mass is a probability. So expresses_weights = True, row_stochastic = True, and Mega is the member of the state-space lineage that the decomposition studies can actually score.

Omitted. Mega's output gates (sigmoid-weighted residual mixing) and its single-head shared-representation projections are not modelled: they act elementwise on y after the aggregation, so including them would break Invariant W without changing anything about the measure. The EMA parameters and the q/k smoothing are what the bank models. The EMA is kept unidirectional (causal) even when causal=False, so that the chunk boundary is the only thing the flag moves.

No softmax anchor is declared. objective = MODIFY: Mega was never an approximation of dense attention. It happens to contain one — switch the EMA off and remove the chunking and the operator is softmax — and tests/test_recurrent_ssm.py uses that as a correctness check, but declaring it as limit_config would claim fidelity to softmax as Mega's goal, which is not what the paper proposes.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default chunk 8 ndim 2 ema True seed 0

chunk: attention span in positions (None = one chunk, i.e. no chunking).

ndim is the EMA's expansion — the dimension of the state carried per feature, Mega's h — and ema=False removes the moving average, leaving the chunked attention alone.

ab.describe("mega")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chunk, ema, ndim, support_size.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    c = min(n if self.chunk is None else self.chunk, n)
    return {"flops": 4 * (m + n) * d * max(self.ndim, 1) + 2 * m * c * (d + dv),
            # one ndim-dimensional EMA state per feature, plus one chunk of KV
            "state_bytes": (2 * max(self.ndim, 1) * d + c * (d + dv)) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 3,145,728 268,435,456 0.0117× state_bytes 2,560 262,144 0.00977× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("mega", chunk=8, ndim=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

MegaAttention(name='mega', category='recurrent', objective='modify', backend='reference', chunk=8, ema=True, ndim=2, seed=0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chunk, ema, ndim, support_size], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
extras: ['chunk', 'ema', 'ndim', 'support_size']

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with mega removed.

changes the same object — recurrent decay_rnn, delta_rnn, gla, hgrn2, hyena, linear_rnn, lru, mlstm, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, recurrent only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, gqa, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, lowrank_ot, mla, otke, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, sinkhorn, unbalanced_sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, modify only

docs.title: CaM
docs.text:
merge_cam · ab.build("merge_cam")

CaM: the token leaving the cache is merged into its neighbours instead of dropped.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.CaMAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/merge_cam.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, sec:compress-merge, prop:compress-noeviction. CaM sits on a StreamingLLM cache — sinks attention sinks plus a recent window of recent = budget - sinks — and asks what to do with the token that falls off the back of the window. Eviction throws it away. CaM writes its value into the next merge_window entries first:

rho_j   = pi(j) / mean_{j < i <= j + recent} pi(i)        (clamped to [0, 1])
g_j     ~ Bernoulli(rho_j)
v_hat_i += g_j v_hat_j / merge_window,   j < i <= j + merge_window

rho_j is the prominence of the departing token relative to the window it is leaving, so a token nobody looked at is usually dropped and a heavy hitter is usually carried. Because v_hat_j on the right is the already-merged value, a token that is carried and then itself evicted cascades further forward; running the loop in increasing j on a mutable value field reproduces that exactly, as the released code does by mutating value_states in place.

What CaM does and does not preserve. Keys are never merged, so the measure is a plain renormalised restriction: extras['eps'] is the mass CaM deletes, and setting merge_window = 0 — the same method with the repair switched off — deletes it bit for bit and leaves v alone. What CaM repairs is the value field: v_hat != v, and the evicted values survive inside the retained ones. This is therefore not the pushforward of merge_kv, where the mass itself is carried and pi_hat picks up the log |C_i| gauge bias; it is a restriction with a repaired v_hat, and eq:error_decomposition splits it that way — CaM leaves the distributional term exactly where eviction left it and attacks the value term alone. Saying so is the point: the two repairs are different objects, and tests/test_compress_evict.py measures both.

Semantics: eviction, with a destructive twist. The merge pass is the prefill: the whole stream is ingested, the cache is reduced to budget, and every query is then served from that one reduced, rewritten cache — which is why the method declares supports_causal = False. The twist is that the damage is worse than hiding in a way no member of restrict/ can imitate: sink_window leaves v untouched, so a later pass can still read the original values, whereas CaM has overwritten them. The cache cannot be un-merged.

mode defaults to 'expected', which uses rho_j itself as the gate — the conditional expectation of the released code's Bernoulli draw. The bank's conformance suite requires a method to agree between fp32 and fp64 and between CPU and CUDA, and a coin flip on a threshold does not; mode='sample' reproduces the released sampler through a seeded torch.Generator for anyone who wants the variance.

Exact limit: budget = None (nothing leaves the window, nothing is merged).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
parameter default budget 6 sinks 2 merge_window 4 obs 4 mode 'expected' seed 0

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with budget=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("merge_cam").limit_config
{'budget': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: assign, budget, chi2, cluster_radius, eps, k_realized, merge_gate, merge_window, prominence, recent, retained_idx, sinks, sizes, support, v_bar.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    b = max(1, min(self.budget or n, n))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * b * (d + dv) + n * dv,
            "state_bytes": b * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * b * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 1,638,400 268,435,456 0.0061× state_bytes 1,536 262,144 0.00586× bytes_moved 1,835,008 4,718,592 0.389×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("merge_cam", budget=6, sinks=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["merge_cam"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"merge_cam": {'budget': 6, 'sinks': 2}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Token merging
docs.text:
merge_kv · ab.build("merge_kv")

Token merging: a pushforward compression of the context measure.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.MergeKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/merge_kv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-merge, prop:compress-merge, prop:error-merge. A partition C_1, ..., C_r of the positions and the map T: x -> cluster(x) define

mu_hat = T_# mu,    mu_hat({i}) = mu(C_i),
y_hat(q) = sum_i mu(C_i) e^{beta <q, k_hat_i>} v_hat_i / sum_i mu(C_i) e^{beta <q, k_hat_i>},

i.e. ToMe's proportional attention: the merged token carries the mu-mass of its preimage, which in log form is the log |C_i| bias. Without it the pushforward is replaced by counting measure on the compressed domain and large clusters are systematically under-weighted.

Expressing it on the original positions. Lift the representatives back, k~_j = k_hat_{T(j)} and v~_j = v_hat_{T(j)}; then pi~_j ∝ e^{beta <q, k~_j>} on the original n positions satisfies pi~ @ v~ = y_hat and sum_j pi~_j = 1. The multiplicity appears automatically, because a cluster of size |C_i| contributes |C_i| identical atoms. That is the sense in which the pushforward is mass-preserving, and it is what tests/test_compress.py checks.

Representatives. k_hat_i and v_hat_i are the within-cluster means. The paper notes this is not the right key representative even for one query: the exact contribution is mu(C_i) exp(Lambda_i(q)) with Lambda_i the log-MGF of the cluster's keys, and by Jensen mean-key merging under-weights every cluster, to leading order by exp(-beta^2 q^T Sigma_i q / 2). The within-cluster covariance is returned in extras so that correction can be studied.

Not causal: clusters span positions on both sides of a query.

Exact limit: n_clusters = None (singleton clusters).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_clusters 6 mode 'contiguous' seed 0

mode: 'contiguous' (consecutive tokens) or 'kmeans' (on keys).

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_clusters=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("merge_kv").limit_config
{'n_clusters': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The compressed context is built by this method, and the measure it reports lives on the original \(n\) positions — a kernel run over the compressed cache would return neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: assign, cluster_radius, k_bar, sizes, v_bar.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = min(self.n_clusters or n, n)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * r * (d + dv) + 2 * n * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + r * 4,      # + multiplicities
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + r * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 1,835,008 268,435,456 0.00684× state_bytes 1,560 262,144 0.00595× bytes_moved 263,680 4,718,592 0.0559×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("merge_kv", n_clusters=6, mode='contiguous')
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["merge_kv"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"merge_kv": {'n_clusters': 6}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: ToMe
docs.text:
merge_tome · ab.build("merge_tome")

ToMe: bipartite soft matching — the pushforward whose partition is matched.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ToMeAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/merge_tome.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-merge, prop:compress-merge, prop:error-merge. merge_kv already implements the pushforward mu_hat = T_# mu and ToMe's proportional attention; what it does not implement is ToMe's actual choice of T. Contiguous blocks ignore similarity and Lloyd's algorithm is iterative and order-dependent; ToMe's point was that a single round of bipartite matching is almost as good and costs one matrix product:

  1. split the current tokens alternately into A (even slots) and B (odd slots);
  2. draw one edge from each a in A to its most cosine-similar b in B, using the attention keys as the metric;
  3. keep the r heaviest edges;
  4. merge each matched a into its b by averaging, and concatenate back.

A round can remove at most half the tokens, so reaching a target of n_clusters takes ceil(log2(n / n_clusters)) rounds; ToMe spends them one per transformer layer, this file spends them inside one call, which is the same map. The matching is greedy and deterministic — no seed, unlike merge_kv(mode='kmeans').

Mass. Exactly as in merge_kv: the representatives k_hat_i, v_hat_i are the within-cluster means and are lifted back to the original n positions, so

pi~_j ∝ e^{beta <q, k_hat_{T(j)}>},   sum_j pi~_j = 1,   pi~ @ v~ = y_hat,

and a cluster of size |C_i| contributes |C_i| identical atoms — ToMe's + log s proportional-attention term, appearing automatically rather than by hand. Dropping it would replace T_# mu by counting measure on the compressed domain. extras carries assign, sizes and cluster_radius so that metrics.merge_bound applies, and v_bar so it can be called directly.

One deviation, stated rather than hidden. ToMe merges tokens of the residual stream, so a single partition is shared by every head. Here each (batch, head) matches on its own keys, which keeps the head independence the conformance suite checks (DESIGN.md Sec. 4, check 5) and makes the method comparable with the rest of compress/; assign is therefore [B, H, n] and merge_bound is applied per slice.

Not causal: a cluster spans positions on both sides of a query.

Exact limit: n_clusters = None (no edge is kept; every token is its own cluster).

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_clusters 6

n_clusters: how many tokens survive; None merges nothing.

ab.describe("merge_tome")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_clusters=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("merge_tome").limit_config
{'n_clusters': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The compressed context is built by this method, and the measure it reports lives on the original \(n\) positions — a kernel run over the compressed cache would return neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: assign, cluster_radius, k_bar, sizes, v_bar.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = max(1, min(self.n_clusters or n, n))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * r * (d + dv) + n * n * d // 2,   # + the matching
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + r * 4,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + r * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 35,127,296 268,435,456 0.131× state_bytes 1,560 262,144 0.00595× bytes_moved 263,680 4,718,592 0.0559×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("merge_tome", n_clusters=6)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["merge_tome"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"merge_tome": {'n_clusters': 6}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Multi-head latent attention
docs.text:
mla · ab.build("mla")

Multi-head latent attention: one joint low-rank KV latent, per-head up-projection.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.MLAAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/mla.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-arch. Instead of caching h key–value pairs per position, MLA caches a single latent c_j = W_down [k_j^{(1)}; ...; k_j^{(h)}; v_j^{(1)}; ...] of dimension r, and reconstructs each head's key and value by a per-head up-projection. The cached state per position drops from h (d + d_v) to r.

Like GQA this is an operator modification trained as such; it is in the library for the roofline (it is the other intervention that raises decode arithmetic intensity) and because it is the cleanest example of a compression that couples heads: the latent is shared, so head_independent = False.

The projections are trained in DeepSeek-V2. Here W_down is a fixed seeded Gaussian and the up-projection is its pseudo-inverse, so the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection onto row(W_down). That choice is data-independent, hence causal, and makes the exact limit provable: at r = h (d + d_v) the matrix is square and invertible, the reconstruction is exact, and the operator is dense softmax.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent no it shares \(K\)/\(V\) across query heads, so heads are not independent. trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default r 16 seed 0 sdpa_kernel None

r: latent width; None uses the full width (the exact limit).

ab.describe("mla")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with r=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("mla").limit_config
{'r': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default sdpa torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention -- on CUDA, FlashAttention-2 or the memory-efficient kernel

Each non-reference entry is a claim that the path is equal to the reference, and tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence checks it on five shapes, both causal settings, float32 and float64. See Backends.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2, heads: int = 1):
    wide = heads * (d + dv)
    r = min(self.r or wide, wide)
    per_head = n * r * bytes_per_el / max(1, heads)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * n * r * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": per_head,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + per_head}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 272,629,760 268,435,456 1.02× state_bytes 32,768 262,144 0.125× bytes_moved 294,912 4,718,592 0.0625×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("mla", r=16)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

MLAAttention(name='mla', category='compress', objective='modify', backend='reference', r=16, sdpa_kernel=None, seed=0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=[1, 2, 64, 32], extras=[latent, latent_width, r], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. The mLSTM is the one member of this family that keeps a denominator, and keeping it is the whole reason it is here:

C_t = f_t C_{t-1} + i_t v_t k_t^T,            C_t in R^{d_v x r}   (matrix memory)
n_t = f_t n_{t-1} + i_t k_t,                  n_t in R^r           (normaliser)
y_hat_t = C_t q_t / max(|n_t^T q_t|, 1),

with i_t = exp(i~_t) an exponential input gate and f_t = sigmoid(f~_t) a scalar forget gate — so A_t = f_t Id, data-dependent but not diagonal: one rate for the whole head, unlike GLA. The interest is entirely in the second and third lines. n_t is the same recurrence driven by k_t instead of k_t v_t^T, so n_t^T q_t is exactly the row sum of the unnormalised weights: the mLSTM carries the denominator of eq:attention_expectation as part of its state, which linear attention threw away and which linear_rnn does not have.

It still does not get the contract back, and the max(., 1) is why. Dividing by max(|n_t^T q_t|, 1) makes the readout bounded — that was the goal, since an exponential input gate can make the true denominator astronomically small — but it is not division by the mass. When the mass exceeds one the operator is normalised and the row sums to one; when it does not, the row is left alone and sums to less. Row sums are therefore in [0, 1] and the weights are signed (q_t . k_t is a raw inner product), so normalization invariance and constant preservation fail exactly in the small-mass regime, which is reported in extras["clipped"]. That partial restoration is a sharper illustration of sec:memory-state than dropping the normaliser outright: the denominator is present and the invariant still breaks.

Exponential gating needs the paper's stabiliser or it overflows at the first large logit. With c = cumsum(log f),

m_t = max_{j <= t} ( log i_j + c_t - c_j ) = c_t + cummax( log i - c )_t,

and every stabilised coefficient a_{tj} = exp(log i_j + c_t - c_j - m_t) lies in (0, 1] by construction. The denominator floor becomes exp(-m_t) in the same units. This is the recurrence m_t = max(log f_t + m_{t-1}, log i_t) of the paper, written as the prefix scan it is.

The gates. A trained mLSTM reads i~_t and f~_t off x_t through learned projections. With no training this reference takes two fixed orthogonal directions of the key — the mean <k_t, 1>/sqrt(d) for forgetting and the alternating-sign direction <k_t, (-1)^c>/sqrt(d) for writing — plus the biases below. They are stand-ins, stated rather than hidden; what matters downstream is that both gates are scalar per head and functions of the token, and both are.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default forget_bias 3.0 input_bias 0.0 state_rank None

forget_bias shifts f~ (positive = remember longer, the LSTM default).

input_bias shifts i~. state_rank truncates the key/query dimension and so is the size of the matrix memory, state_rank x d_v plus the state_rank of the normaliser; None keeps all d channels.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.
