docs.title: ReBased
docs.text:
rebased · ab.build("rebased")

ReBased: a learnable quadratic feature map with a movable root.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.ReBasedAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/rebased.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-det. Aksenov et al. (2024) start from the observation that Based's surrogate 1 + z + z^2/2 has minimum 1/2 at z = -1: however negative the logit, the weight it assigns is bounded below, so the measure can never concentrate the way softmax does. Their fix keeps the quadratic but makes its root learnable — normalize each head's queries and keys, then apply a per-channel affine before squaring,

phi(q) = (gamma_Q . norm(q) + beta_Q)^2,   phi(k) = (gamma_K . norm(k) + beta_K)^2,
g_hat(q, x) = <phi(q), phi(k_x)>,   y_i = phi(q_i)^T sum_j phi(k_j) v_j^T
                                         / phi(q_i)^T sum_j phi(k_j),

with norm a LayerNorm over the head dimension (no affine of its own: gamma and beta are that affine, learned separately for queries and keys) and . the elementwise product. phi >= 0 is a square, so pi_hat is a probability measure, and phi now reaches zero — at norm(x)_c = -beta_c / gamma_c — which is the whole point.

This is an operator modification: r = d features, no resource parameter, and no configuration under which it becomes softmax, so both correctness anchors are None by design (tab:kernel-methods). Two structural consequences follow from the normalization and are worth separating from the learnability. First rem:kernel-homogeneous applies exactly: LayerNorm discards ||q||, so unlike based — and unlike softmax — scaling the query cannot sharpen pi_hat_q at all. Second, g_hat is a quadratic form in norm(q), hence bounded on the sphere: the dynamic range of the surrogate is bounded uniformly in the input, where exp is not. Both are visible in extras.

gamma and beta are the learned parameters, so trainable = True. The defaults are their initialization, gamma = 1 and beta = 0, at which phi(x) = norm(x)^2; pass floats to move them (the same value in every channel) and see the root move with them.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default gamma_q 1.0 beta_q 0.0 gamma_k 1.0 beta_k 0.0 
ab.describe("rebased")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: Z_hat, dynamic_range, g_hat, phi_k, phi_q.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = d
    return {"flops": 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv + 4 * (m + n) * r,
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 17,301,504 268,435,456 0.0645× state_bytes 8,320 262,144 0.0317× bytes_moved 532,608 4,718,592 0.113×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("rebased", gamma_q=1.0, beta_q=0.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

ReBasedAttention(name='rebased', category='interaction', objective='modify', backend='reference', beta_k=0.0, beta_q=0.0, gamma_k=1.0, gamma_q=1.0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[Z_hat, dynamic_range, g_hat, phi_k, phi_q], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
extras: ['Z_hat', 'dynamic_range', 'g_hat', 'phi_k', 'phi_q']

docs.title: Reformer LSH attention
docs.text:
reformer · ab.build("reformer")

Reformer LSH attention: the support is a hash bucket.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ReformerAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/reformer.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-content ("Content-based supports"). Angular locality-sensitive hashing gives a query-dependent, content-based support that costs O(n d b) to build rather than the O(n d) of the full score row it replaces. With R a random d x (b/2) Gaussian matrix, Reformer's hash is

h(x) = argmax( [x R ; -x R] )  in  {0, ..., b-1},

a random partition of the sphere into b cones whose collision probability P[h(q) = h(k)] = 1 - theta(q, k) / pi decreases with the angle, so the bucket of a query is biased towards its large-score keys. n_rounds independent hashes are drawn and the supports unioned, which raises recall at linear cost — the standard amplification, and the knob Reformer actually reports.

Given the support the operator is the renormalized restriction of prop:sparse-identity: the error is eps_q (m_{S^c} - m_S) with eps_q = pi_q(S^c), exactly as for topk. What LSH buys is that S_q is found without computing pi_q; what it costs is that S_q is not the top-k — collisions are probabilistic, so a heavy key is missed with probability (theta/pi)^n_rounds and light keys are retained. Contrast lsh_sample, which uses the same hashing to build a proposal and reweights by 1/u instead of restricting: that estimator is consistent, this one is biased, and the bias is the omitted mass.

Deviations from the paper, which are about the kernel rather than the operator:

  • Reformer ties queries and keys (k_j = q_j / ||q_j||) so that one hash serves both and a position always collides with itself. The bank's queries and keys are independent, so both are hashed with the same R and the query's own position is added to its support unconditionally — which is what tying makes automatic, and what guarantees a nonempty row. With shared QK the two agree.
  • Reformer then sorts by bucket and attends within fixed-size chunks (plus the previous chunk), to bound memory and to handle uneven buckets. That is a batching device: the set it approximates is the one implemented here, "keys sharing a bucket with the query in at least one round". hyperattention does implement a sorted, block-structured version of the same idea.
  • Reformer masks a position from attending to itself when it has other options, an artifact of shared QK that does not apply here.

Exact limit: n_buckets = 1 puts every key in the query's bucket, so the support is the whole visible context and pi_hat = pi.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_buckets=1 this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("reformer").limit_config
{'n_buckets': 1}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: bucket_k, bucket_q, chi2, collision_rate, eps, k_realized, n_buckets, n_rounds, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    half = max(1, self.n_buckets // 2)
    kept = max(1.0, n / max(1, 2 * half)) * self.n_rounds
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * d * half * self.n_rounds + 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 69,206,016 268,435,456 0.258× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 67,502,080 4,718,592 14.3×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("reformer", n_buckets=8, n_rounds=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["reformer"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"reformer": {'n_buckets': 8, 'n_rounds': 2}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

ReformerAttention(name='reformer', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', n_buckets=8, n_rounds=2, seed=0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[bucket_k, bucket_q, chi2, collision_rate, eps, k_realized, n_buckets, n_rounds, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)

docs.title: Retention (RetNet)
docs.text:
retnet · ab.build("retnet")

Retention (RetNet): a multi-scale fixed decay, one time constant per head.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.RetNetAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/retnet.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences (row "Retention"). The recurrence is

S_n = gamma S_{n-1} + k_n v_n^T,      y_hat_n = S_n^T q_n,

and its parallel form is the one the paper writes,

Retention(X) = (Q K^T * D) V,    D_{nm} = gamma^{n-m} for n >= m, else 0,

so A_t = gamma Id is a scalar multiple of the identity and does not depend on the input. That is the whole content of the row: retention is the input-independent member of this family, and everything after it (GLA, HGRN2, RWKV-6, the mLSTM) is the same recurrence with A_t made a function of x_t.

What decay_rnn does not already cover is the multi-scale part. RetNet runs h heads at h different time constants,

gamma = 1 - 2^{-5 - arange(0, h)},

so head 0 keeps a half-life of about 22 tokens and head h-1 is almost lossless. A single scalar gamma — decay_rnn — has to choose one point on that curve; the head schedule is how RetNet gets a range of recency priors out of one operator at one state size, which is exactly the recency-versus-capacity separation study S6 is after. Pass decay= to collapse the schedule back to one rate and recover decay_rnn with the identity feature map.

Two further differences from decay_rnn, both from the paper. The interaction is the raw scaled inner product <q_t, k_j> / sqrt(d), with no positive feature map, so the weights are signed; and the readout carries no denominator, so the rows do not sum to one. The effective mass is still bounded by 1 / (1 - gamma) rather than growing with n — boundedness without normalization, the distinction sec:memory-state draws. normalize=True puts the denominator back.

xPos relative position embedding, the GroupNorm on the readout and the swish gate are part of the RetNet block, not of the retention operator, and are left out: this file is the operator of tab:memory-recurrences.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default decay None base_exponent 5 normalize False state_rank None

decay: one rate for every head; None uses the paper's head schedule.

base_exponent is the 5 in gamma_h = 1 - 2^{-5-h}. state_rank truncates the key/query dimension, which is the size of the recurrent state (state_rank x d_v); None keeps all d channels.

ab.describe("retnet")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: decay, gamma, half_life, mass, state_rank.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.state_rank or d
    return recurrent_cost(m, n, r, dv, bytes_per_el)

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,842,752 268,435,456 0.0627× state_bytes 8,192 262,144 0.0312× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("retnet", base_exponent=5, normalize=False)

docs.title: Routing Transformer
docs.text:
routing · ab.build("routing")

Routing Transformer: the support is a learned cluster.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.RoutingAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/routing.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-content ("Content-based supports"). Where reformer partitions the sphere at random and topk reads the true scores, routing places c centroids in the query/key space and lets a query attend to the keys routed to its centroid:

r(x) = argmax_i  <x / ||x||, mu_i>,    S_q = { j : r(k_j) = r(q) }  (and the
                                               query's own position),

so the support costs O((m + n) c d) to compute and the partition is shared across queries rather than recomputed per query. Given S_q the operator is again the renormalized restriction of prop:sparse-identity. Optionally w > 0 adds a sliding window, because the published model combines content routing with local attention and attributes part of its result to the combination.

The centroids are trained. In the paper they are parameters updated by online k-means: an exponential moving average of the queries and keys assigned to each centroid, carried across minibatches, with the centroids re-normalized to the sphere. They are never fitted to the sequence being attended to, and they could not be — doing so inside a causal decode would let the support of an early query depend on later keys. This class therefore declares trainable = True, and its untrained behaviour is the paper's initialization: c directions drawn from a seeded standard Gaussian and normalized. That is a random partition of the sphere into Voronoi cones, which is a lower bound on what routing buys — it is roughly reformer with one round and cones that are not axis-paired, and it should be read as the floor the training is supposed to lift, not as the method's accuracy. Pass centroids= a [c, d] tensor to supply trained ones; the forward pass is the same either way.

Load balance. The published implementation takes, per cluster, the n/c keys with the largest centroid dot product, so that every cluster has the same size and the attention can be batched as a dense c x (n/c) tensor. Nearest-centroid membership — what is implemented here — is the routing rule that device approximates; it leaves clusters uneven, which is visible in extras["k_realized"] and is part of what the selector costs.

Exact limit: n_clusters = 1 routes everything to one centroid, so S_q is the whole visible context and pi_hat = pi.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    c = max(1, self.n_clusters)
    kept = max(1.0, n / c) + 2 * self.w + 1
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * d * c + 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": (n * (d + dv) + c * d) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + c * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv)
                           * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 68,419,584 268,435,456 0.255× state_bytes 262,656 262,144 1× bytes_moved 67,764,736 4,718,592 14.4×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: RWKV-5/6 time mixing
docs.text:
rwkv · ab.build("rwkv")

RWKV-5/6 time mixing: a matrix-valued state that the current token bypasses.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.RWKVAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/rwkv.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. Eagle (RWKV-5) and Finch (RWKV-6) write the time-mixing step as

wkv_t = S_{t-1} + Diag(u) k_t v_t^T,       S_t = Diag(w_t) S_{t-1} + k_t v_t^T,
y_hat_t = wkv_t^T q_t,                     w_t = exp(-exp(d_t)) in (0, 1)^r,

which is the family's recurrence with two deliberate departures.

The state is matrix-valued. RWKV-4 carried a per-channel numerator and denominator — 2d numbers, a diagonal operator, no mixing between channels. Eagle replaces the element-wise product by the outer product k_t v_t^T and the state becomes r x d_v. That is the same move HGRN2 makes, and for the same reason: at a fixed parameter count prop:memory-rank ties recall to the number of state variables, and r d_v is r times more of them than d.

The current token is not in the state. The readout uses S_{t-1} and adds the token's own write back with a separate bonus gate u. So the decay a key at j suffers is prod_{u = j+1}^{t-1} w_u — lag t - 1 - j, not t - j — and the diagonal weight is u <q_t, k_t> with no decay at all. RWKV is therefore not a pure exponential-recency operator: it has a recency prior plus an always-available present, which is what the bonus term buys. bonus=0 removes it and the method becomes ordinary gated linear attention one step out of phase.

w_{tj} = <q_t, exp(c_{t-1} - c_j) * k_j>     j < t,     c = cumsum(log w),
w_{tt} = u <q_t, k_t>.

Finch versus Eagle. Eagle's decay w = exp(-exp(omega)) is a learned per-channel constant; Finch makes omega a function of the token, w_t = exp(-exp(d_t)). data_dependent=False selects the Eagle form and is the controlled comparison the family exists to make: same state, same bonus, gate input-dependent or not. With no training there is no projection to produce d_t, so this reference uses d_t = decay_base + k_t — stated plainly, and all that is needed of it is that the gate be per channel, in (0, 1), and a function of the token. The double exponential is the paper's and is what keeps log w_t = -exp(d_t) strictly negative and finite however large the logits get.

No denominator survives — RWKV-4's was dropped precisely when the state became a matrix — so the rows are signed and do not sum to one. The LayerNorm, the SiLU gate and the token shift belong to the RWKV block, not to this operator.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default decay_base -2.0 bonus 1.0 data_dependent True normalize False state_rank None

decay_base: the omega of w = exp(-exp(omega + k_t)).

bonus is RWKV's u, the weight the current token gets outside the state. data_dependent=False drops the k_t term and gives Eagle (RWKV-5); True gives Finch (RWKV-6). state_rank truncates the key/query dimension and so is the size of the state, state_rank x d_v.

docs.title: S4D
docs.text:
s4d · ab.build("s4d")

S4D: the diagonal state-space layer, as a long convolution over the values.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.S4DAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/s4d.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. Each value channel carries its own single-input single-output state-space model

h_t^{(c)} = A_c h_{t-1}^{(c)} + B_c v_{t,c},     y_{t,c} = C_c h_t^{(c)},

with A_c = diag(exp(dt_c lambda)) diagonal and stable. Because A, B, C and the step dt are parameters and not functions of the input, the recurrence unrolls into a convolution whose kernel depends on the lag alone,

y_{t,c} = sum_{l >= 0} K_c[l] v_{t-l, c},        K_c[l] = 2 Re sum_n C_{cn} Bbar_{cn} lambdabar_{cn}^l,

and the layer can be evaluated for the whole sequence at once. That input-independence is the property this corner of the library exists to exhibit, and the step that produced the current generation of models — Mamba, GLA, the gated linear RNNs — was precisely to give it up and let A_t depend on x_t.

What is implemented, and what is not. This is S4D (Gu, Gupta, Goel and Re, 2022), the diagonal state-space model, not the full S4 of Gu, Goel and Re (2022), whose state matrix is diagonal-plus-low-rank and whose kernel is evaluated through a Cauchy kernel and a Woodbury correction on the generating function. S4D keeps the diagonal part, drops the low-rank correction — DSS (Gupta et al., 2022) showed that costs nothing in accuracy — and has a closed-form kernel, which is what is coded here. Calling this file s4 would have named something it is not.

It does not read the queries or the keys. An LTI layer mixes positions with a filter indexed by the lag; there is nowhere for q and k to enter. The library keeps the attention signature so that the operator can be put side by side with softmax on identical inputs, and the resulting gap — an SSM of this kind cannot do associative recall at all — is the finding, not a defect of the wrapper. extras['reads_qk'] is False and tests/test_recurrent_ssm.py asserts it.

Weights. expresses_weights = False. Every value channel is convolved with a different kernel, so there is no single measure pi_hat over the n context positions that reproduces the output: the operator mixes positions, but with a different mixture per channel. Manufacturing a weight matrix here would mean averaging kernels across channels and reporting something the method does not compute. The per-channel kernels are returned in extras['kernel'] instead, which is the honest object.

Frequency domain. fft=True evaluates the same convolution with three FFTs, which is how S4 is actually run. It is not the default because an FFT mixes the whole sequence and is therefore not bit-exactly causal — a later value perturbs an earlier output in the last few bits — and the conformance suite checks causality exactly. tests/test_recurrent_ssm.py checks the two paths agree to 1e-10 in fp64.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights no it cannot name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original positions and is excluded from the error decomposition by declaration. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_state 16 init 'lin' dt_min 0.001 dt_max 0.1 fft False seed 0

n_state: poles per channel (each standing for a conjugate pair).

init selects the pole placement, 'lin' (S4D-Lin) or 'inv' (S4D-Inv); dt_min / dt_max bound the log-uniform timestep, which is what sets the range of timescales the channels cover; fft switches to the frequency-domain evaluation (see the module docstring).

ab.describe("s4d")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """Costed as the deployed layer runs: build the kernel, then one FFT convolution."""
    logn = max(1.0, math.log2(max(n, 2)))
    return {"flops": 6 * dv * n * self.n_state + 15 * dv * n * logn,
            # a complex state of N poles for each of the dv channels
            "state_bytes": 2 * self.n_state * dv * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (n * dv + m * dv + 2 * self.n_state * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,121,856 268,435,456 0.0601× state_bytes 4,096 262,144 0.0156× bytes_moved 266,240 4,718,592 0.0564×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: S5
docs.text:
s5 · ab.build("s5")

S5: one diagonal MIMO state-space model, run as a parallel associative scan.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.S5Attention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/s5.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences. S4D gives every channel its own single-input state-space model and evaluates each as a convolution. S5 keeps the diagonal state matrix and makes two simplifications that turn out to matter more than the machinery they replace: one state h_t in C^N is shared by all d_v channels (multi-input multi-output), and the recurrence is evaluated by a parallel scan rather than by an FFT convolution.

h_t = lambdabar * h_{t-1} + Bbar v_t,      y_t = 2 Re(C h_t) + D * v_t,

with lambdabar = exp(dt lambda), Bbar = (lambdabar - 1) lambda^{-1} B, B in C^{N x d_v} and C in C^{d_v x N}. Composing two steps of a diagonal recurrence is an elementwise product, so the affine-map monoid underneath it is cheap and the sequence can be swept in ceil(log2 n) parallel rounds (attnbank.methods.recurrent._ssm_kernels.diagonal_scan). That is the whole S5 contribution, and it is also what made the data-dependent successors possible: a scan does not care whether lambdabar is a parameter or a function of the token, whereas the FFT convolution S4 relies on does.

Here, it is a parameter. lambdabar, Bbar, C and D do not depend on the input, so the operator is still a (now matrix-valued) convolution K[l] = C A^l B in the lag — the family's defining restriction, and the one Mamba lifted.

State. N complex numbers in total, against S4D's N per channel. That is the contrast prop:memory-rank is about and the reason n_state is a plain configuration key: the capacity sweeps vary it.

It does not read the queries or the keys — see s4d for why that is the point rather than an omission. extras['reads_qk'] is False.

Weights. expresses_weights = False. The convolution kernel C A^l B is a d_v x d_v matrix per lag, so the output is not sum_j w_{tj} v_j for any scalar w: the operator mixes channels as well as positions. No measure over the original positions exists to report, and the library says so instead of inventing one.

Simplifications. The poles are placed by the S4D-Lin (or S4D-Inv) closed form, which approximates the spectrum of the normal part of HiPPO-N; S5 obtains them by numerically diagonalising HiPPO-N itself. The two spectra agree in their leading term -1/2 + i pi n, and a closed form keeps the layer deterministic across LAPACK versions. B, C, D and the per-mode timestep are seeded random stand-ins for learned parameters, so trainable = True.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights no it cannot name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original positions and is excluded from the error decomposition by declaration. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable yes it has learned parameters; the reference implementation initialises them from a seed, so the numbers here are an untrained operator.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_state 16 init 'lin' dt_min 0.001 dt_max 0.1 feedthrough True seed 0

n_state: the size N of the single state shared by all channels.

feedthrough keeps S5's D * v_t skip term; init, dt_min and dt_max place the poles and the per-mode timestep exactly as in s4d.

ab.describe("s5")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: None, and that is the declaration. objective = modify means this is a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so neither anchor applies. The conformance suite does not skip the check — it asserts the exemption, requiring limit_config() and convergence_configs() to both be None for a modify method.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A scan over positions with a fixed-size state is a different program from a masked softmax.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: b_bar, c_eff, d_skip, lam, n_state, reads_qk, state_size.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = self.n_state
    return {"flops": 8 * n * r * dv + 8 * n * r + 8 * m * r * dv,
            # ONE complex state of N poles, shared by every channel
            "state_bytes": 2 * r * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (n * dv + m * dv + 4 * r * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 16,908,288 268,435,456 0.063× state_bytes 64 262,144 0.000244× bytes_moved 270,336 4,718,592 0.0573×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("s5", n_state=16, init='lin')
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("expresses_weights =", attn.expresses_weights,
      "-- no measure over the original positions exists,",
      "so weights is", out.weights)
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

S5Attention(name='s5', category='recurrent', objective='modify', backend='reference', dt_max=0.1, dt_min=0.001, feedthrough=True, init='lin', n_state=16, seed=0)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=None, v_hat=None, extras=[b_bar, c_eff, d_skip, lam, n_state, reads_qk, state_size], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0

docs.title: Swin-style shifted local windows
docs.text:
shifted_window · ab.build("shifted_window")

Swin-style shifted local windows: a block-diagonal support, optionally displaced.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ShiftedWindowAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/shifted_window.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-fixed. Unlike the banded support of window, Swin partitions the sequence into non-overlapping windows of w positions and lets each query see only its own window (Liu et al., 2021). Consecutive layers alternate between the regular partition and one "displaced from the regularly partitioned windows by (floor(w/2), floor(w/2)) pixels", which is what connects windows that would otherwise never communicate. In one dimension this is

S_p = { j : floor((j + shift)/w) = floor((p + shift)/w) },

a block-diagonal matrix whose blocks are offset by shift. shift = 0 is the regular partition — plain chunked / block-local attention, the pattern of BlockBERT (Qiu et al., 2020) — and shift = floor(w/2) is Swin's displaced partition; the default follows Swin. Under shift > 0 the first window is a short one of w - shift positions, exactly as in the paper's "efficient batch computation".

The difference from window is the point of having both: at an equal budget w the banded support is query-centred and always keeps the w nearest keys, while the block support keeps between 1 and w of them depending on where in its block the query sits. The shift is what repairs the queries that land at a block boundary, and extras['window_offset'] reports the realised distance to the start of the block so that the effect can be measured rather than argued.

A query is always in its own window, so the diagonal is kept and no row is empty. Intersecting with the causal mask turns this into block-causal attention: query p sees the earlier positions of its own block only. Values are untouched, so the error is eps_q (m_{S^c} - m_S) (prop:sparse-identity); w = None is a single window over the whole sequence and recovers dense softmax exactly.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default w 4 shift None

w: window size (None = one window, the exact limit).

shift: displacement of the partition; None means Swin's floor(w/2), 0 is the regular (block-diagonal) partition.

ab.describe("shifted_window")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with w=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("shifted_window").limit_config
{'w': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, n_windows, shift, support, window_offset, window_size.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    kept = min(n, self.w or n)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": kept * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,   # one resident window
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 1,048,576 268,435,456 0.00391× state_bytes 1,024 262,144 0.00391× bytes_moved 1,310,720 4,718,592 0.278×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("shifted_window", w=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["shifted_window"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"shifted_window": {'w': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

ShiftedWindowAttention(name='shifted_window', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', shift=None, w=4)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chi2, eps, k_realized, n_windows, shift, support, window_offset, window_size], dtype=float32, device=cpu)

docs.title: StreamingLLM
docs.text:
sink_window · ab.build("sink_window")

StreamingLLM: the first s "attention sink" positions plus a sliding window.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.SinkWindowAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/sink_window.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-fixed, sec:compress-evict, ex:sparse-sink. The support is {0, ..., s-1} union {p-w+1, ..., p}: content-independent, and therefore an eviction policy as much as a sparsity pattern.

The reason it works is prop:sparse-identity read backwards. A head that routes mass eps to a sink with a near-null value computes y = (1-eps) m_S; a pure window outputs m_S, an amplification by 1/(1-eps). Retaining the sink restores the normalizer, not information: the sink carries normalization. Comparing sink_window(s>0) with window at the same total budget isolates that effect, which is what makes the pair worth having in the library.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default sinks 2 w 8 
ab.describe("sink_window")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with sinks=0, w=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("sink_window").limit_config
{'sinks': 0, 'w': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, sinks, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    kept = (self.w or n) + self.sinks
    return {"flops": 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": kept * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,621,440 268,435,456 0.00977× state_bytes 2,560 262,144 0.00977× bytes_moved 2,883,584 4,718,592 0.611×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("sink_window", sinks=2, w=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["sink_window"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"sink_window": {'sinks': 2, 'w': 8}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

SinkWindowAttention(name='sink_window', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', sinks=2, w=8)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chi2, eps, k_realized, sinks, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
{'output_error': 1.9121, 'distributional_error': 1.9121, 'value_error': 0.0, 'tv': 0.66426}

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with sink_window removed.

changes the same object — restrict bigbird, blocktopk, hyperattention, longformer, lsh_sample, oval, page_pca, reformer, routing, shifted_window, strided, topk, value_topk (oracle), window  ·  browse the bank, restrict only judged the same way — approximate, beyond the ones above abc, atom, based, clustered, evict_adakv, evict_h2o, evict_pyramidkv, evict_snapkv, evict_tova, favorpp, favorsharp, hedgehog, kivi, kvquant, linformer, lowprec, lowrank_kv, lowrank_logit (oracle), merge_cam, merge_kv, merge_tome, nmf_oracle (oracle), nystrom, performer, polysketch, qjl, quantkv, skyformer, svd_oracle (oracle), trigrff, zipcache  ·  browse the bank, approximate only

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.SinkhornAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/sinkhorn.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot-eot. Softmax attention is semi-relaxed entropic OT: it minimizes int c dgamma + eps KL(gamma || nu x mubar) subject to the row marginal only (prop:ot-gibbs). Adding the column constraint gives entropic OT, and the central structural fact (prop:ot-conditional) is that its conditionals are still softmax — tilted by a query-independent key potential:

pi^OT_q(dx) ∝ exp( beta ( <q, k_x> + psi(x) ) ) mubar(dx).

So a doubly stochastic attention operator is characterised, completely, by one vector psi per context: an economic price that is negative on keys over-subscribed under softmax and positive on under-subscribed ones. extras["potential"] returns the quantity psi in the form in which the identity can be checked directly, pi_hat = softmax_j(s_ij / eps + potential_j), which is what study S7 does.

Sinkhorn's algorithm alternates the two identities of prop:ot-conditional (b) in log domain (eq:ot-sinkhorn): a row log-sum-exp (a softmax normalizer) followed by a column log-sum-exp. One step from psi = 0, stopped after the row update, is exactly softmax attention — so n_iter = 0 is the exact limit, and the whole operator family is a continuation of softmax in the number of iterations.

Not causal, and not by omission: prop:ot-causal shows that a lower-triangular matrix with equal row and column sums is diagonal. Causal attention with uniform marginals is the identity, every token attending only to itself. A non-uniform column marginal satisfying sum_{j>=t} b_j <= sum_{i>=t} a_i is the way out, and is not implemented here.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_iter 5 eps 1.0

n_iter: Sinkhorn iterations (0 = softmax exactly). eps: entropic regularization, applied as a temperature on the scaled logits.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_iter=0, eps=1.0 this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("sinkhorn").limit_config
{'n_iter': 0, 'eps': 1.0}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A fixed-point iteration over the whole matrix is not a kernel call, and the normalisation it computes is not per-query.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: col_marginal, f, g, gamma, marginal_error, n_iter, potential, row_marginal, target_col, target_row.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * self.n_iter * m * n,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + n * 4,   # + the key potential
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv
                            + 2 * self.n_iter * m * n) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 278,921,216 268,435,456 1.04× state_bytes 266,240 262,144 1.02× bytes_moved 21,495,808 4,718,592 4.56×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("sinkhorn", n_iter=5, eps=1.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

SinkhornAttention(name='sinkhorn', category='coupling', objective='modify', backend='reference', eps=1.0, n_iter=5)

invariant W: 0.0

docs.title: Skyformer
docs.text:
skyformer · ab.build("skyformer")

Skyformer: kernelize first, then Nystrom on a matrix that is actually PSD.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.SkyformerAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/skyformer.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-matrix. Nystromformer applies the Nystrom method to P, which is neither symmetric nor PSD, so none of the Nystrom theory applies to it. Skyformer fixes the premise rather than the conclusion, in two steps.

Kernelize. With beta = 1/sqrt(d) the softmax kernel factors through a Gaussian one,

SM(q, x)   = exp(beta <q, k_x>)
           = exp(beta ||q||^2 / 2) * C(q, x) * exp(beta ||k_x||^2 / 2),
C(q, x)    = exp(-beta ||q - k_x||^2 / 2),

i.e. A = D_Q^{1/2} C D_K^{1/2} with (D_Q)_ii = exp(beta ||q_i||^2) (Eq. 1 of the paper). C is the kernelized attention score matrix: the paper's operator is C V, which is already "automatically normalized" and is therefore a different operator — the key factor D_K^{1/2} does not cancel. The bank targets softmax, so this file keeps C as the object that is approximated and then undoes the diagonal: the query factor cancels under row normalization and the key factor is multiplied back in. That is the use the paper states for the same machinery in Sec. 4.2 — "a low-rank approximation to A also implies an approximation to D".

Lift. C is a rectangular block, but it is a block of the Gram matrix of the union of the two point sets, and that matrix is PSD:

Cbar = kappa([Q; K] / d^{1/4}, [Q; K] / d^{1/4}) in R^{(m+n) x (m+n)},
Cbar_tilde = Cbar S (S^T Cbar S)^+ S^T Cbar,
C_tilde    = (I, 0) Cbar_tilde (0, I)^T,

with S a uniform sub-sampling matrix choosing r of the m + n positions. Since ||C - C_tilde|| <= ||Cbar - Cbar_tilde||, approximating the block reduces to approximating a PSD matrix, which is what Nystrom has guarantees for (Theorem 2 of the paper, after Musco and Musco). This is the whole difference from nystrom, and it is a difference in the premise, not in the formula.

What survives and what does not. The core pseudo-inverse makes C_tilde signed, so pi_hat is a signed measure: row_stochastic = False and the output can leave the convex hull of the values. Rows do sum to one here because the library normalizes explicitly, which the paper's own operator does not.

Exact limit. r = None samples every position, S = I, and Cbar Cbar^+ Cbar = Cbar, so C_tilde = C and pi_hat is softmax — for any m and n, since the lift is square by construction. That is the anchor.

Numerics. The whole factorization is float64, and the Gram matrix is scaled by a single positive constant chosen to centre its log-range (Nystrom is homogeneous of degree one, and the scalar cancels in the row normalization). Without it the off-diagonal block underflows to zero in the large-logit regime while the diagonal stays at one — the Gaussian Gram matrix tends to the identity when the points are far apart, which is the regime where this kernelization has nothing left to approximate.

Not causal: the sub-sampling draws landmarks from the whole union, future included.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.text:

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with r=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("skyformer").limit_config
{'r': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: Z_rel, min_weight, n_landmarks, neg_mass.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = min(self.r or (m + n), m + n)
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * r ** 3 + 2 * (m + n) * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (d + dv)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 8,396,800 268,435,456 0.0313× state_bytes 4,096 262,144 0.0156× bytes_moved 528,384 4,718,592 0.112×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("skyformer", r=16)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["skyformer"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"skyformer": {'r': 16}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Dense softmax attention
docs.text:
softmax · ab.build("softmax")

Dense softmax attention: the reference operator, y(q) = sum_j pi_q(j) v_j.

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective accelerate — same operator, exact up to floating point; only the evaluation changes class attnbank.SoftmaxAttention, attnbank/reference.py monograph sec:found

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues acceleration: the operator is the reference operator, exact up to floating point. The only question worth asking of it is where exactness stops.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
pi_q(j) = exp(beta ) / sum_i exp(beta ), beta = 1/sqrt(d)

Everything in the library is compared against this. Section sec:found.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default sdpa_kernel None

sdpa_kernel: pin the SDPA sub-backend (flash / mem_efficient / math) instead of letting torch choose. Ignored by other backends.

ab.describe("softmax")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: This method is exact as built: the conformance suite instantiates it at its default config and requires both y and the weights to match softmax. limit_config() returns {} — the empty dict, not None: there is a limit and no setting has to be changed to reach it.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default sdpa torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention -- on CUDA, FlashAttention-2 or the memory-efficient kernel flash_attn the flash-attn package (CUDA, fp16/bf16)

Each non-reference entry is a claim that the path is equal to the reference, and tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence checks it on five shapes, both causal settings, float32 and float64. See Backends.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv), "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + 2 * m * n) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,435,456 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 4,718,592 4,718,592 1×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("softmax")
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = accelerate: the claim is equality with the reference, so that
# is what the example checks.
y_ref = ab.attend("softmax", q, k, v, causal=True)
print("max |y - y_softmax|:", float((out.y - y_ref).abs().max()))

SoftmaxAttention(name='softmax', category='exact', objective='accelerate', backend='reference', sdpa_kernel=None)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras={}, dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
max |y - y_softmax|: 0.0

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with softmax removed.

changes the same object — exact flash, lowprec, splitk  ·  browse the bank, exact only

Open the browser with softmax selected and tick up to three more to see them in columns. Every row there is one the registry declares, and the rows the selected methods agree on fold away.

docs.title: Split-K / Flash-Decoding
docs.text:
splitk · ab.build("splitk")

Split-K / Flash-Decoding: partition the keys, attend independently, merge by LSE.

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective accelerate — same operator, exact up to floating point; only the evaluation changes class attnbank.SplitKAttention, attnbank/methods/exact/splitk.py monograph sec:exact

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues acceleration: the operator is the reference operator, exact up to floating point. The only question worth asking of it is where exactness stops.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text: sec:exact-tiling (decode-specialized kernels). The context is split into p chunks, each chunk produces a state sigma_{J_t} of def:exact-state, and the states are combined by the monoid of prop:exact-monoid. Parts (i)-(iii) of that proposition say the result is independent of the partition and of the bracketing, which is exactly what tests/test_exact.py checks: every partition, contiguous or not, gives the identical answer.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default splits 4 partition None tree False

partition: an explicit list of index tensors/lists; overrides splits. tree: merge pairwise (a balanced reduction tree) instead of left-to-right.

ab.describe("splitk")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text: This method is exact as built: the conformance suite instantiates it at its default config and requires both y and the weights to match softmax. limit_config() returns {} — the empty dict, not None: there is a limit and no setting has to be changed to reach it.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. The method exists to expose the intermediate states of the evaluation, which a single fused call does not hand back.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: lse, n_splits.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    p = self.splits
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * m * p * dv,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + 2 * m * p * (dv + 2))
                           * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 268,959,744 268,435,456 1× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 1,605,632 4,718,592 0.34×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("splitk", splits=4, tree=False)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = accelerate: the claim is equality with the reference, so that
# is what the example checks.
y_ref = ab.attend("softmax", q, k, v, causal=True)
print("max |y - y_softmax|:", float((out.y - y_ref).abs().max()))

SplitKAttention(name='splitk', category='exact', objective='accelerate', backend='reference', partition=None, splits=4, tree=False)
