docs.title: Sparse Transformer
docs.text:
strided · ab.build("strided")

Sparse Transformer: the strided and fixed factorized patterns.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.StridedAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/strided.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-fixed. Child et al. (2019, Sec. 4.3) factor the attention matrix into two heads whose index sets are, for query i and stride l,

strided:   A_i^(1) = {t, ..., i},  t = max(0, i - l)
           A_i^(2) = {j : (i - j) mod l = 0}

fixed:     A_i^(1) = {j : floor(j/l) = floor(i/l)}
           A_i^(2) = {j : j mod l in {l - c, ..., l - 1}}

with l ~ sqrt(n) and c a small integer (8, 16 or 32 in the paper, for l = 128 or 256). The strided pattern suits data with a natural period — it is the one-dimensional reading of attending to the previous row and the same column of an image — and the fixed pattern suits data without one, where "specific cells summarize previous locations and propagate that information to all future cells".

This method takes the union A_i^(1) u A_i^(2), which is what a single restricted layer can see; the paper's own alternative of giving one head each is a statement about depth, and the bank's unit of measurement is one operator. Both components are stated relative to the query position and then intersected with the mask, so the two-sided reading used in a bidirectional model collapses to Child et al.'s autoregressive sets under causal=True and nothing in the future is ever reachable.

Offset 0 is in both patterns (j = i satisfies (i - j) mod l = 0 and lies in the query's own block), so every row keeps at least the diagonal. stride = 1 makes A^(2) the whole row under either pattern, which is the exact limit.

Values are untouched: the error is eps_q (m_{S^c} - m_S) (prop:sparse-identity). Against longformer this isolates what a periodic support buys over a contiguous one at the same budget — the two keep O(l + n/l) and O(w) keys respectively.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

c: the width of the summarising column of the 'fixed' pattern; ignored by 'strided'.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    l, blocks = self.stride, (n + self.stride - 1) // self.stride
    # strided: l + 1 local and one key per block; fixed: one block and c per block
    kept = min(n, l + 1 + blocks if self.pattern == "strided"
               else l + max(self.c, 1) * blocks)
    return {"flops": 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,   # the column heads reach back
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * kept * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 68,419,584 268,435,456 0.255× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 68,681,728 4,718,592 14.6×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("strided", stride=4, pattern='strided')
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["strided"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"strided": {'stride': 4, 'pattern': 'strided'}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Signed rank bound
docs.text:
svd_oracle · ab.build("svd_oracle")

Oracle — an upper bound, not a method

svd_oracle is not deployable and is not meant to be. It uses information no inference-time method has, and it is in the bank to answer how well could this ever work? — several of the monograph's arguments need that number. Read every result below as a bound on a family of real methods, never as a baseline you could ship.

Signed rank bound: the best rank-r signed factorization of P (truncated SVD).

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.SVDOracleAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/svd_oracle.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-rank. The truncated SVD P_r = U_r Sigma_r V_r^T is the optimal rank-r approximation of P in every unitarily invariant norm (Eckart–Young), so it is the lower bound that no stochastic factorization of the same rank can beat: rank(P) <= rank_+(P) = rank_s(P), and the inequality is usually strict. The gap between this file and nmf_oracle is the empirical nonnegative-rank penalty of study S5.

The price of optimality is the whole contract: P_r is signed, its rows do not sum to one, and the output can leave the convex hull of the values — exactly the failure mode prop:factor-closure was stated to rule out for Markov compositions. row_stochastic = False records it; the row sums and the most negative weight are returned in extras so the violation can be measured instead of assumed.

This is an oracle: no one computes a per-head SVD of P at inference. It exists to bound what any rank-r method could achieve. The decomposition is taken in float64.

Exact limit: r = None keeps the full spectrum. Not causal: the truncation does not preserve the mask's zeros.

Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("svd_oracle", r=4)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["svd_oracle"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"svd_oracle": {'r': 4}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Oracle top-k restriction
docs.text:
topk · ab.build("topk")

Oracle top-k restriction: the k largest true scores, renormalized.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.TopKAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/topk.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-operator, sec:sparse-query. S_q is the set of the k largest exact attention weights, which by prop:error-topk minimizes the omitted mass eps_q — and hence the bound eps_q osc(v) — over all supports of size k. It is the oracle against which every proxy selector (Quest, SparQ, Loki, H2O) is measured: computing all scores saves only the value aggregation.

The proposition's second half matters more for this library: minimizing eps_q is not minimizing ||y - y_hat||. With pi = (0.45, 0.35, 0.20) and scalar values (0, 0, 1), top-2 retains {1,2} and errs by 0.2 while {1,3} omits more mass and errs by 0.11. value_topk is the output-aware alternative; the gap between them is the quantity study S2 reports.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default k 8

k: budget; None keeps every visible key (the exact limit).

ab.describe("topk")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with k=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("topk").limit_config
{'k': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, scores, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    kk = self.k or n
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * d + 2 * m * kk * dv + m * n,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,     # full context stays resident
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + m * kk * dv + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 136,314,880 268,435,456 0.508× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 1,441,792 4,718,592 0.306×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("topk", k=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["topk"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"topk": {'k': 8}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

TopKAttention(name='topk', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', k=8)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chi2, eps, k_realized, scores, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0

docs.title: Random Fourier features for attention
docs.text:
trigrff · ab.build("trigrff")

Random Fourier features for attention: the trigonometric (signed) estimator.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.TrigRFFAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/trigrff.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-rf. Bochner's theorem for the Gaussian kernel plus eq:kernel-softmax-gauss gives the unbiased estimator

xi_omega(q,x) = exp((||qt||^2 + ||kt_x||^2)/2) * cos(omega^T (qt - kt_x)),
omega ~ N(0, I_d),   qt = q/d^{1/4},  kt = k/d^{1/4},

separable with 2r features through cos(a-b) = cos a cos b + sin a sin b. This is the basis of RFA (Peng et al., 2021) and of the trigonometric variant of Choromanski et al. (2021).

Two things go wrong, and this file exists so that they can be measured. (i) The relative variance is 2 sinh^2(||qt - kt_x||^2 / 2) (eq:kernel-trig-var), largest for keys far from the query — the many small entries whose accumulated noise makes Z_hat unreliable. (ii) xi takes both signs, so Z_hat can be zero or negative; then pi_hat is not a probability measure and no bound of the form prop:error-additive holds. The fraction of queries with Z_hat <= 0 is reported in extras["Z_rel"].

Numerics. The factor exp(||kt_j||^2/2) does not cancel in pi_hat and overflows fp32 for large inputs, so the estimator is carried as a (log-magnitude, sign) pair and normalized by attnbank.weights_from_log_magnitude, which subtracts the maximum over the visible keys. When |Z_hat| is below the floor the result is finite but large; this is a reported failure, not a silent repair.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic no the weights are not a probability measure — signed, or not summing to one — so the output can leave the convex hull of the values. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Convergence anchor. There is no finite resource at which this method is exact, so the anchor is monotonicity instead: the mean error against softmax must decrease along these configs, and the suite fails if it does not.

>>> ab.get_class("trigrff").convergence_configs()
[{'r': 8}, {'r': 32}, {'r': 128}, {'r': 512}]

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. sdpa computes exactly \(\mathrm{softmax}(\beta\langle q,k\rangle + \text{mask})\,v\); this operator replaces \(g\), so it is not that expression and there is no kernel for it.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: Z_rel, log_g_hat, negative_Z, r, sign.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    r = 2 * self.r                 # cos and sin halves
    return {"flops": 2 * (m + n) * r * d + 2 * n * r * dv + 2 * m * r * dv,
            "state_bytes": r * (dv + 1) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv + r * (dv + 1)) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 67,108,864 268,435,456 0.25× state_bytes 16,640 262,144 0.0635× bytes_moved 540,928 4,718,592 0.115×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("trigrff", r=64, orthogonal=True)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["trigrff"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"trigrff": {'r': 64, 'orthogonal': True}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

docs.title: Unbalanced entropic OT attention
docs.text:
unbalanced_sinkhorn · ab.build("unbalanced_sinkhorn")

Unbalanced entropic OT attention: the column constraint as a knob, not a law.

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.UnbalancedSinkhornAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/unbalanced_sinkhorn.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot, eq:ot-unbalanced. sinkhorn imposes the column marginal exactly; softmax does not impose it at all. Replacing the hard constraints by Kullback–Leibler penalties puts the two at the ends of one continuum (Frogner et al. 2015; Chizat et al. 2016; Liero et al. 2018; Sejourne et al. 2022):

min_{gamma >= 0}  int c dgamma + eps KL(gamma || nu x mubar)
                  + lam_row KL(gamma_Q || nu) + lam_col KL(gamma_X || mubar).

Chizat et al. show the scaling iterations keep the form of eq:ot-sinkhorn with each potential update damped by rho_i = lam_i / (lam_i + eps):

f <- rho_row ( log a - LSE_j ( s + g ) ),
g <- rho_col ( log b - LSE_i ( s + f ) ),     s = -c/eps.

rho = 1 is the hard constraint of sinkhorn; rho = 0 drops the constraint and leaves the potential at zero. The default here keeps the row constraint hard (lam_row = None, meaning lam_row = infinity), which is what makes the operator a probability measure per query, and treats lam_col as the single dial the paper describes: at lam_col = 0 this is exactly softmax — the semi-relaxed problem of prop:ot-gibbs with psi = 0 — and as lam_col -> infinity it is the doubly stochastic coupling of prop:ot-conditional.

That is why this file, alone among the coupling methods, declares a limit_config even though its objective is MODIFY: the family contains softmax at an interior value of its own parameter. The operator it defines away from that value is still a different operator, not an approximation of softmax, so no convergence sequence is claimed and fidelity is not the goal.

The practical reading is the one sec:ot gives: lam_col interpolates between "sinks allowed" and "sinks forbidden". A finite lam_col lets a key still absorb more than its share — attention sinks survive, in proportion — while bounding how far it can go, and it does so without the abstention mass that a dustbin introduces (dustbin_sinkhorn is the discrete alternative).

extras matches sinkhorn key for key — potential, f, g, gamma, row_marginal, col_marginal, marginal_error — because the plan is still of Gibbs form exp(s + f + g) and prop:ot-conditional still applies verbatim: the conditional is softmax tilted by one number per key. Only the number is different, and col_kl, the divergence the penalty charges, is added.

Not causal, and the relaxation does not rescue it. prop:ot-causal is the limiting obstruction — at lam_col = infinity a triangular doubly stochastic plan is the identity — but at any lam_col > 0 there is a second, more basic one: the column potential g_j is a reduction over all queries that can see key j, including queries later than the one being answered, so the conditional of query i moves when a key after i changes. That is leakage, not degeneracy, and the conformance suite measures it directly. Only at lam_col = 0, where the operator is softmax, does it vanish; supports_causal is one declaration for the whole class, so False is the one that is true of it.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default n_iter 10 eps 1.0 lam_col 1.0 lam_row None

lam_col: KL penalty on the column marginal. 0 is softmax exactly, inf (or a large value) is the doubly stochastic plan of sinkhorn. lam_row: penalty on the row marginal; None means infinity, the hard constraint that keeps every query's conditional a probability measure. eps: entropic regularization, a temperature on the scaled logits. n_iter: scaling iterations.

ab.describe("unbalanced_sinkhorn")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with lam_col=0.0, eps=1.0 this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("unbalanced_sinkhorn").limit_config
{'lam_col': 0.0, 'eps': 1.0}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. A fixed-point iteration over the whole matrix is not a kernel call, and the normalisation it computes is not per-query.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: col_kl, col_marginal, f, g, gamma, lam_col, marginal_error, n_iter, potential, rho_col, rho_row, row_marginal, target_col, target_row.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * self.n_iter * m * n,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + n * 4,   # + the key potential
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv
                            + 2 * self.n_iter * m * n) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 289,406,976 268,435,456 1.08× state_bytes 266,240 262,144 1.02× bytes_moved 42,467,328 4,718,592 9×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("unbalanced_sinkhorn", n_iter=10, eps=1.0)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = modify: this is a different operator and fidelity to softmax
# is not its goal, so there is no error to quote. What it *is* doing shows
# up in its own diagnostics.
print("row_stochastic =", attn.row_stochastic, "| first row sums:",
      [round(x, 4) for x in out.weights.sum(-1)[0, 0, :4].tolist()])
print("extras:", sorted(out.extras))

UnbalancedSinkhornAttention(name='unbalanced_sinkhorn', category='coupling', objective='modify', backend='reference', eps=1.0, lam_col=1.0, lam_row=None, n_iter=10)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[col_kl, col_marginal, f, g, gamma, lam_col, marginal_error, n_iter, potential, rho_col, rho_row, row_marginal, target_col, target_row], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0
row_stochastic = True | first row sums: [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
extras: ['col_kl', 'col_marginal', 'f', 'g', 'gamma', 'lam_col', 'marginal_error', 'n_iter', 'potential', 'rho_col', 'rho_row', 'row_marginal', 'target_col', 'target_row']

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:
Two relations, because the registry declares two axes: what a method changes, and what it is trying to be. Both lists are ab.available(...) with unbalanced_sinkhorn removed.

changes the same object — coupling dustbin_sinkhorn, espformer, lowrank_ot, otke, sinkhorn  ·  browse the bank, coupling only judged the same way — modify, beyond the ones above cosformer, decay_rnn, delta_rnn, gla, gqa, hgrn2, hyena, isab, latent_stochastic, latte, linear_elu, linear_rnn, lru, mega, mla, mlstm, perceiver, polaformer, rebased, retnet, rwkv, s4d, s5  ·  browse the bank, modify only

docs.title: Output-aware selection
docs.text:
value_topk · ab.build("value_topk")

Oracle — an upper bound, not a method

value_topk is not deployable and is not meant to be. It uses information no inference-time method has, and it is in the bank to answer how well could this ever work? — several of the monograph's arguments need that number. Read every result below as a bound on a family of real methods, never as a baseline you could ship.

Output-aware selection: the support that minimizes output error, chosen greedily.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ValueTopKAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/value_topk.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-operator ("Score-optimal is not output-optimal"), prop:error-topk, and the open problem of sec:open-retrieval. Top-k minimizes the omitted mass eps_q and therefore the bound eps_q osc(v); it does not minimize the error. The right target, named in the text, is

min_{|S| <= k}  eps_S ||m_{S^c} - m_S||.

That objective simplifies. For a renormalized restriction y_hat = m_S, so with W_S = pi(S) and U_S = sum_{j in S} pi_j v_j,

eps_S ||m_{S^c} - m_S|| = ||y - m_S|| = ||y - U_S / W_S||,

i.e. the objective is just the realised output error, and no conditional mean of the complement needs to be formed.

Selection. Forward greedy alone is badly myopic here: its first pick minimizes ||y - v_j|| and so can seed the support with a light outlier that later additions cannot undo. The selector therefore evaluates four cheap candidate supports and keeps, per query, whichever realises the smallest error:

  1. score top-k (so the result is never worse than topk, by construction);
  2. forward greedy from the empty set;
  3. forward greedy seeded with the single heaviest position;
  4. backward greedy from the full set, deleting the position whose removal costs least — the elementary step of every eviction policy, and exactly prop:error-single.

Complexity. Each greedy step scores all n candidates, and a candidate is scored in O(d_v) from the running (U_S, W_S) rather than by recomputing the conditional mean, so a forward pass is O(n k d_v) per query and the backward pass O(n (n - k) d_v) — the naive form of either is O(n^2 k). All queries are processed in parallel, at a peak memory of B H m n d_v; pass chunk to process the query axis in slices if that is too large.

None of this is optimal: exhaustive=True enumerates every support of size k (guarded by max_subsets) and gives the true minimum, which is what tests/test_restrict.py uses to bound the greedy gap.

This is an oracle: it reads v and the exact pi_q, which no deployed selector can. Its purpose is to upper-bound what output-aware selection could buy, so correctness matters and speed does not.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with k=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("value_topk").limit_config
{'k': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, selector, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    kk = self.k or n
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * d + 2 * m * n * kk * dv + 2 * m * kk * dv,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 1,209,008,128 268,435,456 4.5× state_bytes 262,144 262,144 1× bytes_moved 524,288 4,718,592 0.111×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("value_topk", k=8, exhaustive=False)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["value_topk"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"value_topk": {'k': 8, 'exhaustive': False}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

ValueTopKAttention(name='value_topk', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', chunk=None, exhaustive=False, k=8, max_subsets=200000)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chi2, eps, k_realized, selector, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0

docs.title: Sliding-window (banded) attention
docs.text:
window · ab.build("window")

Sliding-window (banded) attention: a query-position-dependent, content-free support.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.WindowAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/window.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-fixed. Query at absolute position p attends to {p - w + 1, ..., p}, intersected with what the mask allows. The diagonal is always included, so no row is ever empty.

Applied to a dense-trained model this is an approximation whose error is exactly eps_q (m_{S^c} - m_S) (prop:sparse-identity); it is the cleanest demonstration of the sink effect of ex:sparse-sink, because once the window has scrolled past position 0 it omits a large mass whose conditional mean is the sink value, and renormalization inflates the remaining weights by 1/(1 - eps_q). Compare with sink_window, which differs only by the first s positions.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default w 8

w: window width; None is the full context (the exact limit).

ab.describe("window")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with w=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("window").limit_config
{'w': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    w = self.w or n
    return {"flops": 2 * m * w * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": w * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,     # rolling buffer
            "bytes_moved": (m * d + m * w * (d + dv) + m * dv) * bytes_per_el}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 2,097,152 268,435,456 0.00781× state_bytes 2,048 262,144 0.00781× bytes_moved 2,359,296 4,718,592 0.5×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("window", w=8)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True,
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["window"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                 configs={"window": {'w': 8}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

WindowAttention(name='window', category='restrict', objective='approximate', backend='reference', w=8)
AttentionOutput(y=[1, 2, 64, 32], weights=[1, 2, 64, 64], v_hat=None, extras=[chi2, eps, k_realized, support], dtype=float32, device=cpu)
invariant W: 0.0

docs.title: Related methods
docs.text:

docs.title: ZipCache
docs.text:
zipcache · ab.build("zipcache")

ZipCache: bit width allocated per token by a normalised attention score.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ZipCacheAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/zipcache.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-quant, and the place where this family meets sec:compress-evict. KIVI, KVQuant and Atom all spend the same number of bits on every token. ZipCache does not: it ranks tokens by how much attention they actually receive and gives the salient ones bits_salient while the rest get bits_regular. Eviction is the degenerate case of this — zero bits for the unsalient — and prop:compress-noeviction applies to the ranking either way.

Two ideas, and the second is the one worth implementing carefully.

Channel-separable token-wise quantization. Each channel is first divided by its own maximum absolute value over tokens, then whole tokens are quantized with a single scale, then the channel normalizer is multiplied back: a_c = max_j |x_jc|, x_hat_j = a * Q_b(x_j / a).

What this buys is relative precision, channel by channel. A plain per-token scale is set by whichever channel is largest in that token, so every channel is given the same absolute step and the small channels — the ones a query may well load on — are obliterated. Dividing by a_c first makes the step proportional to each channel's own scale, so the relative error is near-uniform. It is not a smaller Frobenius error, and the test file says so. The side information is d + 2n numbers rather than the 2 n d / g of a group-wise scheme.

The normalised attention score. The usual saliency, sum_i A_ij accumulated down a column, is biased twice over by the causal mask: an early token appears in more rows, and the rows it appears in are shorter, so their softmax puts more mass on each entry. Both biases reward position rather than content. ZipCache divides by the number of queries that could see the token: p_j = sum_i A_ij / nnz(A_{.,j}), nnz(A_{.,j}) = #{i : j <= i + (n - m)}.

The saliency is always measured on the causally masked prefill attention, whatever causal is for the forward pass itself, because that is the quantity a prefill actually has; nnz is then a genuine correction rather than the constant m a non-causal matrix would give.

probe enables the paper's cheap approximation: estimate the column sums from a sample of query rows (half the most recent, half drawn uniformly) instead of the whole matrix, which is what makes the metric compatible with a kernel that never materialises A. probe = None uses every row and is the exact metric.

Not causal. The channel normalizers pool over tokens, and the salient set is chosen after seeing the whole prompt and then applied to every query — the prefill-then-decode pattern of evict_snapkv, and like it, something that cannot be written as one causally masked pass.

Quantize–dequantize is simulated in the input dtype; nothing is actually stored smaller, and cost() states what would be.

target restricts the quantizer to the keys or to the values. The paper quantizes both with the same allocation; the split exists because the error decomposition of sec:output_error — the distributional term against the value term — can only be run on a scheme whose two halves can be switched off independently, and this family is the one that decomposition was written for.

Exact limit: bits_salient = bits_regular = None.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with bits_salient=None, bits_regular=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("zipcache").limit_config
{'bits_salient': None, 'bits_regular': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It returns both the exact and the perturbed score matrices (s, s_hat) in extras — the perturbation is the object of study, and a fused kernel hands back neither.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: accumulated, delta_k, delta_v, s, s_hat, saliency, salient.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    """Two bit widths mixed by ``salient``, one scale per token, one per channel."""
    bs = (self.bits_salient or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    br = (self.bits_regular or 8 * bytes_per_el) / 8
    bits = self.salient * bs + (1.0 - self.salient) * br
    side = (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + 4 * n * bytes_per_el     # a_c, plus 2 per token
    probe = m if self.probe is None else max(1, int(round(self.probe * m)))
    return {"flops": 2 * m * n * (d + dv) + 2 * probe * n * d,
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bits + side,
            "bytes_moved": m * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + n * (d + dv) * bits + side}

At \(m = 1024\), \(n = 1024\), \(d = 64\), \(dv = 64\) and bytes_per_el=2, against the reference operator at the same shape:

quantity this method softmax ratio flops 402,653,184 268,435,456 1.5× state_bytes 57,600 262,144 0.22× bytes_moved 319,744 4,718,592 0.0678×

A cost model is not a benchmark

These are counted operations and resident bytes, not measured time. They are what the monograph's capacity arguments are made of; examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py walks through the comparison properly.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import torch, attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
b, h, n, d = 1, 2, 64, 32
q, k, v = (torch.randn(b, h, n, d) for _ in range(3))

attn = ab.build("zipcache", bits_salient=4, bits_regular=2)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=False,   # it declares supports_causal = False
           return_weights=True)

print(attn)
print(out)
print("invariant W:", out.check_invariant(v))

# objective = approximate: it targets dense softmax, so it is judged by
# output error -- split into the distributional and value terms.
row = ab.compare(["zipcache"], q, k, v, causal=False,
                 configs={"zipcache": {'bits_salient': 4, 'bits_regular': 2}})[0]
print({key: round(row[key], 5) for key in
       ("output_error", "distributional_error", "value_error", "tv")})

ZipCacheAttention(name='zipcache', category='compress', objective='approximate', backend='reference', bits_regular=2, bits_salient=4, probe=None, salient=0.5, seed=0, target='kv')
